Note 1: BUSINESS AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Business Overview
Katapult Holdings, Inc. (“Katapult Holdings,” the “Company," “we,” “our,” or “us”) is a scaled, technology and data-driven platform serving nonprime consumers seeking greater financial flexibility. On December 11, 2025, the Company entered into an Agreement and Plan of Merger (the “Merger Agreement”) with CCF Holdings, LLC ("CCFI"), Aaron’s Intermediate Holdco, Inc. ("Aaron’s") and two wholly owned indirect subsidiaries of the Company, Katapult Merger Sub 1, Inc. and Katapult Merger Sub 2, LLC, pursuant to which those subsidiaries merged with and into Aaron's and CCFI, respectively (the "Mergers"). Upon completion of the Mergers on August 11, 2026 (the "Merger Date"), CCFI and Aaron’s became wholly owned indirect subsidiaries of the Company. Under the terms of the Merger Agreement, equityholders of CCFI and Aaron’s received shares of the Company’s common stock, resulting in a change of control of the Company upon closing. The Mergers were accounted for as reverse mergers using the acquisition method of accounting, pursuant to Accounting Standards Codification ("ASC") Topic 805, Business Combinations (“ASC 805”), with Katapult Holdings treated as the legal acquirer of CCFI and Aaron's and CCFI treated as the accounting acquirer of Katapult Holdings (pre-merger) and Aaron’s. See Note 2 for additional information regarding the Mergers and related agreements.
Through its CCFI, Aaron's, and Katapult operating brands, the Company provides access to alternative consumer financial services and lease-to-own ("LTO") and retail solutions, bringing together proprietary data, technology and underwriting capabilities, retail and e-commerce capabilities, a nationwide physical footprint and customer-focused financial solutions to provide consumers with the tools they need to navigate everyday life.
Consumer Finance Segment
CCFI is a provider of alternative financial services to unbanked and underbanked consumers that operates under various brands including TitleMax, Speedy Cash, CheckSmart and Community Choice Financial. CCFI owns and operates 1,588 retail locations in 25 states and is licensed to deliver similar financial services over the internet in 29 states as of September 30, 2026. Through its network of retail locations and over the internet, CCFI provides customers a variety of financial products and services, including secured and unsecured, short-term and medium-term consumer loans, check cashing, prepaid debit cards, and other services that address the specific needs of its individual customers.
Lease-to-Own and Retail Segment
Aaron's wholly owns The Aaron's Company, Inc. and is a leading, technology-enabled, omnichannel provider of LTO and retail purchase options of furniture, electronics, appliances, and other home goods across its brands: Aaron's and BrandsMart U.S.A. ("BrandsMart"). Aaron's provides consumers with LTO and retail purchase options through the Company's approximately 1,160 Aaron's owned and franchised stores and showrooms in the United States and Canada and the aarons.com e-commerce platform. BrandsMart is a leading appliance and consumer electronics retailer in the southeast United States and one of the largest appliance retailers in the country with 11 stores in Florida and Georgia and a growing e-commerce presence on brandsmartusa.com and other internet marketplaces.
Katapult, one of the Company’s operating brands, is a technology-driven LTO platform that integrates with omnichannel retailers and e-commerce platforms to provide nonprime consumers in the U.S. with access to everyday durable goods. Consumers who may be unable to access traditional financing can choose LTO at checkout with integrated retailers, or shop a growing network of merchants through Katapult’s mobile app marketplace and check out using its innovative Katapult Pay (“KPay”) feature.
Reverse Merger and Basis of Presentation
The accompanying condensed consolidated financial statements as of and for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, and the comparable prior‑year periods, reflect the financial position, results of operations, and cash flows of the Company and its wholly owned subsidiaries, with intercompany balances and transactions eliminated, and have been prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP.

As CCFI was deemed the accounting acquirer under reverse merger accounting, the historical financial statements of CCFI became the historical financial statements of the Company upon the consummation of the Mergers. As a result, the financial statements included in this report reflect (i) the historical operating results of CCFI and its consolidated subsidiaries prior to August 11, 2026 (the presentation of which includes reclassifications to conform to the financial statement presentation of the Company subsequent to the Mergers); (ii) the consolidated results of the Company (including the operations of Katapult, CCFI and Aaron's) from the August 11, 2026 closing date forward; (iii) the assets and liabilities of CCFI at their historical cost; (iv) the assets acquired and liabilities assumed of Aaron's and Katapult Holdings (pre-merger) at fair value from the Merger Date; and (v) the Company’s equity structure for all periods presented.
In accordance with applicable guidance, the equity structure has been restated in all comparative periods to reflect the number of shares of the Company's common stock issued to CCFI unitholders in connection with the Mergers as if such shares had been held since the beginning of the earliest period presented. Further, shares issued to Katapult Holdings' and Aaron's stockholders in connection with the Mergers are treated as consideration transferred and are included in shares outstanding prospectively from the date of the Mergers.
The preparation of the Company's condensed consolidated financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP for interim financial information requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the amounts reported in these financial statements and accompanying notes. Actual results could differ from those estimates.
The accompanying unaudited condensed consolidated financial statements do not include all information required by U.S. GAAP for complete financial statements. In the opinion of management, all adjustments considered necessary for a fair statement have been included in the accompanying unaudited condensed consolidated financial statements. The results of operations for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026 are not necessarily indicative of operating results that may be achieved for another interim period or for the full year.
Within the financial statements and tables presented, certain columns and rows may not add due to the use of rounded numbers for disclosure purposes. Percentages presented are calculated from the underlying whole-dollar amounts.
Seasonality
The Consumer Finance segment experiences fluctuating demand for its lending products throughout the year. Historically, the highest demand for its credit products occurs during the fourth quarter of each calendar year. Conversely, the segment typically observes reductions in finance receivables during the first quarter of each calendar year, primarily due to customers receiving income tax refunds. As a result, Consumer Finance typically experiences higher cash usage in the fourth quarter and increased cash generation in the first quarter, excluding other capital usage.
The Lease-to-Own and Retail segment experiences moderate seasonal fluctuations in revenue as a result of consumer spending patterns. Historically, revenue is strongest for this segment during the first quarter primarily due to higher gross originations during the fourth quarter holiday season. First quarter revenue is also impacted by the federal and state income tax refunds that customers receive, which in the past, has led to customers more frequently exercising the early purchase option on their lease agreements.
Due to the seasonal nature of the business, results of operations for any fiscal quarter may not be indicative of the results for the full fiscal year. Additionally, external factors, such as changes in interest rates and inflation, may influence customer behavior, potentially altering the seasonal patterns typically observed in our business.
Geographic Concentration Risk
The Company’s portfolio of finance receivables is comprised of loan agreements with customers in 31 states and consequently such customers’ ability to honor their contracts may be affected by economic conditions in those states. Additionally, the Company is subject to regulation by federal and state governments that affect the products and services provided by the Company. To the extent that laws and regulations are passed that affect the Company’s ability to offer loans or similar products in any of the states in which it operates, the Company’s financial position could be adversely affected.
During the nine months ended September 30, 2026, the Company operated in 29 states in the United States. As of both September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, gross finance receivables within the Company's three largest states accounted for approximately 47% of the Company's gross finance receivables balance.

Accounting Policies and Estimates
Revenue Recognition
See Note 6 to these condensed consolidated financial statements for further information regarding the Company's revenue recognition policies and disclosures.
Lease Merchandise
The Company’s lease merchandise is recorded at the lower of depreciated cost, including overhead costs from our fulfillment centers, or net realizable value. For the Aaron's operations, the Company begins depreciating furniture and appliances at the earlier of the lease date or 24 months and one day from its purchase, while all other categories of lease merchandise, such as electronics, begin depreciating at the earlier of when the merchandise is leased to the customer or 12 months and one day from its purchase. Lease merchandise fully depreciates over the lease agreement period when on lease, generally 12 to 24 months, and generally 36 months when not on lease. Depreciation is accelerated upon early payout.
For the Katapult operations, the Company utilizes an income forecasting method to evaluate the patterns of the Company’s historical lease merchandise portfolio to apply depreciation rates to the Company’s current lease merchandise portfolio. Lease merchandise is depreciated in the proportion of expected rents received to total expected rents to be received based on the Company’s historical data of lease performance, which includes depreciation for items leased for the full lease duration, accelerated depreciation for early payouts and impairments. The Company also considers other qualitative factors, such as current and forecasted customer payment trends, and other risk-based factors as a component of its forecasting methodology.
The following is a summary of lease merchandise, net of accumulated depreciation and allowances:

The Aaron's store-based operations' policies require weekly merchandise counts at its store-based operations, which include write-offs for unsalable, damaged, or missing merchandise inventories. Monthly cycle counting procedures are performed at the Aaron's fulfillment centers. The Company also monitors merchandise levels and mix by division, store, and fulfillment center, as well as the average age of merchandise on hand. If obsolete merchandise cannot be returned to vendors, its carrying amount is adjusted to its net realizable value or written off. Generally, all merchandise not on lease is available for lease or sale. On a monthly basis, all damaged, lost or unsalable merchandise identified is written off and is included as a component of the provision for lease merchandise write-offs within cost of lease revenues in the accompanying condensed consolidated statements of operations.
For the Aaron's operations, the Company records a provision for write-offs using the allowance method, which is included within lease merchandise, net within the condensed consolidated balance sheets. The allowance method for lease merchandise write-offs estimates the merchandise losses incurred but not yet identified by management as of the end of the accounting period based primarily on historical write-off experience. Other qualitative factors are considered in estimating the allowance, such as seasonality and the impacts of uncertainty surrounding inflationary and other economic pressures in the current macroeconomic environment. Therefore, actual lease merchandise write-offs could differ from the allowance. The provision for write-offs is included in cost of lease revenues in the accompanying condensed consolidated statements of operations. The Company writes off lease merchandise on lease agreements for its Aaron’s operations that are 60 days or more past due on pre-determined dates twice monthly.

NOTES TO UNAUDITED CONDENSED CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
(dollars in thousands, except per share data)


Following the Mergers and as further discussed in Note 2, the Company's lease merchandise was recorded at estimated fair value on August 11, 2026. As a result, the allowance for lease merchandise write-offs was $0 on that date and approximately $2.6 million at September 30, 2026. The allowance only includes a provision for lease merchandise write-offs for lease originations subsequent to August 11, 2026.
Merchandise Inventories, net
The Company’s merchandise inventories are stated at the lower of weighted average cost or net realizable value, and consist entirely of merchandise held for sale by BrandsMart. In-bound freight-related costs from vendors, net of allowances and vendor rebates, are included as part of the net cost of merchandise inventories. Costs associated with storing and transporting merchandise inventories to our retail stores are expensed as incurred and included within cost of merchandise sales in the condensed consolidated statements of operations.
The Company periodically evaluates aged and distressed inventory and establishes an inventory markdown which represents the excess of the carrying value over the amount the Company expects to realize from the ultimate sale of the inventory. Markdowns establish a new cost basis for the inventory and are recorded within cost of merchandise sales within the condensed consolidated statements of operations. The write-offs of merchandise inventories associated with the Company's cycle and physical inventory count processes are also included within cost of merchandise sales in the condensed consolidated statements of operations. The Company records an inventory reserve for the anticipated loss associated with selling inventories below cost. This reserve is based on management’s current knowledge with respect to inventory levels, sales trends, and historical experience selling or disposing of aged or obsolete inventory.
Following the Mergers and as further discussed in Note 2, the Company's merchandise inventory was recorded at estimated fair value on August 11, 2026. As a result, the reserve for merchandise inventories was $0 on that date and was not material as of September 30, 2026.
Cost of consumer finance revenues
Included in the cost of consumer finance revenues are fair value adjustment of finance receivables, net charge-offs of finance receivables at fair value and the provision for credit losses.
For short-term unsecured consumer loans, the Company’s policy is to charge off loans when they become past due. For short-term unsecured installment consumer loans, the Company's policy is to charge off loans when accounts are sixty days past due. The Company’s policy dictates that, where a customer has provided a check or an electronic payment authorization for presentment upon the maturity of a loan, the Company will deposit the customer’s payment for the amount due. If the check or draft is returned as unpaid, all accrued fees and outstanding principal are charged-off as uncollectible. For short-term secured loans, the Company’s policy generally requires that balances be charged off when accounts are either thirty, sixty or ninety days past due depending on the product.

For medium-term secured and unsecured consumer loans, the Company’s policy requires that balances be charged off when accounts are either sixty or ninety days past due.

The amount of the resulting charge-off may include unpaid principal, accrued interest and any uncollected fees, if applicable. Recoveries of amounts previously charged off are recorded to the allowance for credit losses or the accrual for third-party losses in the period in which they are received.
Fair value adjustment of finance receivables: Represents the change in fair value of all of the Company's finance receivables at fair value. Such receivables include all newly originated loans under medium-term secured and medium-term unsecured products since July 1, 2024, excluding products tied to a line of credit and any third-party lender products under a credit service organization ("CSO") program, which share similarities in classifications of term length and securitization, but differ in terms of financial instrument product type.
Net charge-offs of finance receivables at fair value: Represents the charge-off of past due balances on any of the Company's finance receivables at fair value, net of recovered finance receivable principal and related fees.
Provision for credit losses: Represents provisions for credit losses on the Company's finance receivables at amortized cost, net, in amounts sufficient to maintain an adequate allowance for credit losses and an adequate accrual for losses related to guaranteed loans processed for third-party lenders under a CSO program. The provision for credit losses was $134.7 million and $135.5 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively and $348.5 million and $336.9 million during the nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively.

Finance receivables at amortized cost, net
Finance receivables consist of short-term and medium-term secured and unsecured consumer loans. For secured loans, the customer provides collateral which the Company has the right to operate or sell if the customer is experiencing financial difficulty. Secured consumer loans are generally secured by automobiles, motorcycles, or other personal property. There are no modifications to customers experiencing financial difficulty. In certain states, in compliance with law, the Company offers an extended payment plan for all borrowers. Gross loan receivables subject to these repayment plans were immaterial at both September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025.
Short-term consumer loans can be unsecured or secured with a maturity up to ninety days. Unsecured short-term loan products typically range in principal from $50 to $825, with a maturity between fourteen and thirty-five days. This form of lending is based on applicable laws and regulations which vary by state. The Company accrues interest on past-due loans until charged-off for most short-term loans. The customers repay the loan by making cash payments or allowing a check or preauthorized debit to be presented. Secured consumer loans with a maturity of ninety days or less are included in this category and represented 80.8% and 80.5% of short-term consumer loans at September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, respectively.
Medium-term consumer loans can be unsecured or secured with a maturity greater than ninety days and up to forty-eight months. Unsecured medium-term products typically range from $50 to $6,000 and are evidenced by a promissory note with a maturity between three and thirty-six months. These consumer loans vary in structure depending upon the applicable laws and regulations where they are offered. The Company accrues interest on past-due loans until charged-off for most medium-term loans. For most title loans, the interest and fee income is suspended if the loan is delinquent over thirty-five days and is not resumed until the loan is current. The medium-term consumer loans are payable in installments or provide for a line of credit with periodic payments. Secured consumer loans with a maturity greater than ninety days are included in this category and represented 37.8% and 41.7% of medium-term consumer loans at September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, respectively.
Allowance for Credit Losses
Provisions for credit losses included in cost of consumer finance revenues on the Company's condensed consolidated statements of operations are charged to income in amounts sufficient to maintain an adequate allowance for credit losses and an adequate accrual for losses related to guaranteed loans processed for third-party lenders under a CSO program. The factors used in assessing the overall adequacy of the allowance for credit losses on finance receivables, the accrual for losses related to guaranteed loans made by third-party lenders and the resulting provision for credit losses include an evaluation by product based on historical loss experience. The Company evaluates various qualitative factors that may or may not affect the computed initial estimate of the allowance for credit losses on finance receivables, by using internal valuation inputs including historical loss experience, delinquency, overall portfolio quality, and current economic conditions.

Management estimates the allowance balance using relevant information relating to past events, current expectations related to economic conditions, and reasonable and supportable forecasts. Due to the short-term nature of the loan portfolio, forecasted changes in the macroeconomic variables such as unemployment levels and inflationary pressures typically do not have a significant impact on loans outstanding. The Company utilizes a loss rate approach in determining its lifetime expected credit losses primarily based on the Company’s historical loss experience. The forecast of expected losses by loss curves as compared to historical loss curves identifies significant changes in borrower behavior that may indicate historical loss rates should be adjusted, and extends over a reasonable and supportable forecast period. Due to the short-term nature of the loan portfolio, the reversion back to historical loss rates after the forecasting period does not have a meaningful impact and does not require reversion adjustments. The Company’s current expected credit loss (“CECL”) vintage model segments its loan portfolio into monthly pools of receivables by short-term, medium-term, secured and unsecured and estimates the allowance for credit losses by applying loss rates primarily derived from internal, historical cumulative loss experience, then adjusted by qualitative factors to address recent and forecasted business trends. Qualitative factors considered when determining any adjustments to the historical loss rates included, but were not limited to, contractual delinquency, the value of underlying collateral, economic and other qualitative considerations, and management’s judgment. The Company evaluates such pooling decisions and adjusts as needed from time to time as risk characteristics change. While management uses the best information available to make its evaluation, future adjustments to the allowance for credit losses may be necessary if there are significant changes in economic conditions.
The Company’s policy is to charge off loans when they become past due. Depending on the length and type of loan, balances are generally charged off when accounts are between thirty and ninety-one days past due.
The Company may place loans on nonaccrual status due to statutory requirements, or if the timely collection of principal and interest becomes uncertain. Accrued interest is not applied against interest income and loans remain on nonaccrual status until payment or charge-off. The Company had $95.7 million and $94.5 million of loans in nonaccrual status as of September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, respectively.
The amount of charge-offs for past due short-term and medium-term secured and unsecured loans may include unpaid principal, accrued interest not otherwise reversed and any uncollected fees, if applicable. Recoveries of amounts previously charged off are recorded to the allowance for credit losses or the accrual for third-party losses in the period in which they are received. Charge-off and recovered finance receivable revenues are included in cost of consumer finance revenues in the Company’s condensed consolidated statements of operations.
Finance receivables at fair value
As adopted, on July 1, 2024, the Company elected the fair value option (“FVO”) under ASC 825-10, to be applied to all newly originated loans under medium-term secured and medium-term unsecured products, excluding products tied to a line of credit and any third-party lender products under a CSO program, which share similarities in classifications of term length and securitization, but differ in terms of financial instrument product type. As such, the respective finance receivables are reported as finance receivables at fair value on the Company’s consolidated balance sheets. The FVO portfolio is measured based on a discounted cash flow methodology. Loss and payment activity and certain cost assumptions are determined using respective historical data and include consideration of recent trends and anticipated future performance. Future cash flows are discounted using a rate of return that the Company believes is reflective of the market. Interest and fee income on finance receivables at fair value are included in consumer finance revenues in the Company’s condensed consolidated statements of operations.
Secured consumer loans before fair value adjustments with a maturity greater than ninety days included in this category represented 77.2% and 78.0% of medium-term consumer loans at September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, respectively.
Credit service organization
Certain subsidiaries of the Company offer a CSO product to assist customers in obtaining credit with unaffiliated third-party lenders for a fee. The Company records a liability for the secured and unsecured loans expected to default subject to a guarantee. This liability is included in accounts payable and accrued liabilities on the Company’s condensed consolidated balance sheets.

The accrual for third-party credit losses is estimated using relevant information relating to past events, current expectations related to economic conditions, and forecasts. The Company utilizes a loss rate approach in determining its lifetime expected credit losses primarily based on third-party lender historical loss experience. The Company’s CECL vintage model segments its loan portfolio into monthly pools of receivables by short-term, medium-term, secured and unsecured and estimates the accrual for credit losses by applying loss rates primarily derived from internal, historical cumulative loss experience, then adjusted by

Sales Taxes
The Company applies the net basis for sales taxes imposed on goods and services in the condensed consolidated statements of operations. The Company is required by the applicable governmental authorities to collect and remit sales taxes. Accordingly, such amounts are charged to the customer, collected, and remitted directly to the appropriate jurisdictional entity.
Estimated Claims Liability Costs
Estimated claims liability costs are accrued primarily for workers compensation and vehicle liability as well as general liability and group health insurance benefits provided to team members. These liabilities are recorded within insurance related liabilities within accounts payable and accrued liabilities in the condensed consolidated balance sheets. Estimates for these claims liabilities are made based on actual reported but unpaid claims and actuarial analysis of the projected claims run off for both reported and incurred but not reported claims. This analysis is based upon an assessment of the likely outcome or historical experience and considers a variety of factors, including the actuarial loss forecasts, company-specific development factors, general industry loss development factors and third-party claim administrator loss estimates of individual claims.
The Company makes periodic prepayments to its insurance carriers to cover the projected claims run off for both reported and incurred but not reported claims, considering its retention or stop loss limits. In addition, the Company has prefunding balances on deposit and other insurance receivables with the insurance carriers which are recorded within prepaid expenses and other assets in our condensed consolidated balance sheets.

Recent Accounting Pronouncements
Adopted
In July 2025, the Financial Accounting Standards Board ("FASB") issued Accounting Standards Update ("ASU") No. 2025-05, "Financial Instruments - Credit Losses (Topic 326): Measurement of Credit Losses for Accounts Receivable and Contract Assets" ("ASU 2025-05"). ASU 2025-05 provides a practical expedient that allows entities to assume conditions existing as of the balance sheet date remain unchanged over the life of the asset when estimating credit losses for current trade receivables and current contract assets arising from transactions accounted for under Topic 606. The amendments are effective on a prospective basis for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2025, and for interim periods within those fiscal years, with early adoption permitted. The Company adopted this ASU on January 1, 2026 on a prospective basis and did not elect the practical expedient. The adoption of ASU 2025-05 did not have a material impact on the Company's condensed consolidated financial statements.
Not Yet Adopted
In November 2024, the FASB issued ASU 2024-03, "Disaggregation of Income Statement Expenses" ("ASU 2024-03"). ASU 2024-03, among other items, requires additional financial statement disclosures in tabular format disaggregating information about prescribed categories (including employee compensation, depreciation and amortization) underlying any relevant income statement expense captions. ASU 2024-03 is effective on a prospective basis for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2026, and interim periods within fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2027, with early adoption and retrospective application permitted. The Company is currently evaluating the impact this guidance will have on the disclosures within our condensed consolidated financial statements.
In September 2025, the FASB issued ASU 2025-06, "Intangibles—Goodwill and Other—Internal-Use Software (Subtopic 350-40): Targeted Improvements to the Accounting for Internal-Use Software" ("ASU 2025-06"). ASU 2025-06 updates requirements for capitalizing internal-use software costs by replacing the current stage-based model with a principles-based approach. Under ASU 2025-06, the prescriptive software development stages (e.g., preliminary project stage, application development stage) are eliminated, and instead capitalization must begin when management authorizes and commits to funding the project and it is probable the project will be completed and used as intended. ASU 2025-06 is effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2027, including interim periods within those fiscal years, with early adoption permitted. ASU 2025-06 may be applied prospectively, on a modified retrospective basis for in-process projects, or retrospectively. The Company is currently evaluating the impact this guidance will have on our condensed consolidated financial statements and related disclosures.
In November 2025, the FASB issued ASU 2025-08, "Financial Instruments – Credit Losses (Topic 326)" to expand the gross-up approach in Topic 326 at the time of acquisition to certain acquired non-PCD loans that are deemed “seasoned” as defined in the ASU. The amendments are effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2026, and interim reporting periods within those annual reporting periods. The amendments must be applied prospectively and early adoption is permitted. The Company is evaluating the impact of this ASU but does not expect these amendments to have a material effect on the condensed consolidated financial statements.
In December 2025, the FASB issued ASU 2025-11, Interim Reporting (Topic 270): Narrow-Scope Improvements which adds clarity and guidance to the application of Topic 270, including a principle to disclose material events since the most recent annual reporting period. The amendments are effective for interim reporting periods within annual reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2027, for public business entities and for interim reporting periods within annual reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2028, for entities other than public business entities. The amendments can be applied prospectively or retrospectively, and early adoption is permitted. The Company is evaluating the impact of this ASU but does not expect these amendments to have a material effect on the condensed consolidated financial statements.

Note 2: ACQUISITIONS
On December 11, 2025, the Company entered into a merger agreement with CCFI, Aaron’s, and two wholly owned indirect subsidiaries of the Company, pursuant to which those subsidiaries merged with and into Aaron's and CCFI, respectively. The transaction closed on August 11, 2026. Upon completion of the Mergers, CCFI and Aaron’s became wholly owned indirect subsidiaries of the Company. Under the terms of the Merger Agreement, equityholders of CCFI and Aaron’s received shares of the Company’s common stock, resulting in a change of control of the Company upon closing. We believe the Mergers provided a compelling opportunity to create a premier omni-channel platform that provides non-prime consumers access to durable goods and a comprehensive suite of innovative financial solutions tailored to their specific needs.
The Mergers were accounted for as reverse mergers using the acquisition method of accounting, pursuant to ASC Topic 805, Business Combinations (“ASC 805”), with Katapult Holdings treated as the legal acquirer of CCFI and Aaron's and CCFI treated as the accounting acquirer of Katapult Holdings (pre-merger) and Aaron’s. CCFI has been determined to be the accounting acquirer primarily based on an evaluation of the following facts and circumstances: (i) previous CCFI unitholders have the largest portion of voting rights in the combined organization, holding approximately 80.0% of the shares of the combined entity on a fully diluted basis, (ii) CCFI controls the Board of Directors of the combined organization with six of the ten-member board being designees selected by CCFI, including the Executive Chairman of the Board being the previous CCFI Executive Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer, and (iii) CCFI was the largest of the three entities when considering net income and enterprise value.
In connection with the Mergers, the Company incurred $19.5 million and $24.8 million of acquisition-related costs during the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, consisting primarily of professional and consulting fees and transaction-related compensation costs, which are included in selling, general and administrative expense within the condensed consolidated statements of operations.
ASC 805 requires the allocation of the purchase price consideration to the fair value of the identified assets acquired and liabilities assumed upon consummation of a business combination. Accordingly, the total purchase price to acquire Aaron’s and Katapult Holdings has been preliminarily allocated to the assets acquired and assumed liabilities of Aaron’s and Katapult Holdings based upon their estimated fair values. Any excess amounts, after allocating the purchase consideration to identifiable tangible and intangible assets acquired and liabilities assumed, have been recorded as goodwill. The net assets of CCFI continue to be recognized at historical cost.
Consideration Transferred
The fair value of consideration transferred has been determined based on the number of Katapult Holdings' common shares issued or retained and the per share opening price of Katapult Holdings’ common stock as of August 11, 2026 on NASDAQ, as the quoted market price is more readily determinable and a more reliable indicator of fair value than the per unit price of CCFI units, as CCFI, the accounting acquirer, was a private entity prior to the Mergers.

Preliminary Purchase Price Allocation
The fair values of the assets acquired and liabilities assumed, including the consideration transferred, are based on the Company’s best estimates and assumptions using the information available as of the acquisition date through the date of this filing. The primary areas of the preliminary acquisition accounting that are not yet finalized include, but are not limited to, the following: (i) finalizing the review and valuation of intangible assets, including key assumptions, inputs and estimates, (ii) finalizing the Company's estimate of the impact of acquisition accounting on deferred income taxes or liabilities, (iii) finalizing the Company's review of certain working capital accounts acquired/assumed, (iv) finalizing the allocation of goodwill to the Company's reporting units and (v) finalizing the evaluation and valuation of certain legal matters and/or other loss contingencies, including those that the Company may not yet be aware of but that meet the requirement to qualify as a pre-acquisition contingency. The preliminary purchase price allocation remains subject to revision during the measurement period, which may not exceed one year from the acquisition date, as additional information becomes available concerning facts and circumstances that existed as of the acquisition date. Actual values may differ (possibly materially) when final information becomes available that differs from our current estimates. We believe that the information gathered to date provides a reasonable basis for estimating the preliminary fair values of assets acquired and liabilities assumed. The Company expects to finalize the valuation as soon as practicable, but no later than one year from the acquisition date. Goodwill primarily represents expected synergies from combining the businesses, assembled workforce and future growth opportunities. None of the goodwill attributable to the Mergers is expected to be deductible for tax purposes.

Note 4: FAIR VALUE MEASUREMENT
Fair value is defined as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. The Company classifies its financial instruments within the fair value hierarchy based on the lowest level of input that is significant to the fair value measurement. The hierarchy is as follows:
Level 1 — Quoted prices (unadjusted) in active markets for identical assets or liabilities that the Company can access at the measurement date.
Level 2 — Inputs other than quoted prices included within Level 1 that are observable for the asset or liability, either directly or indirectly. These inputs include quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets or quoted prices for identical or similar assets or liabilities in markets that are not active.
Level 3 — Unobservable inputs for the asset or liability that are used when observable inputs are not available, which require the Company to develop its own assumptions.

The FVO portfolio is measured at fair value on a recurring basis pursuant to the Company's election of the fair value option under ASC 825 for these receivables. The fair value of these finance receivables is estimated using a discounted cash flow methodology that incorporates significant unobservable inputs, such as estimated loss, payment activity, discount rate, and certain originating, servicing, and collection cost assumptions that are unobservable but reflect the Company's best estimates of the assumptions a market participant would use to calculate fair value. As the model inputs are based on significant unobservable inputs, the FVO portfolio is classified as Level 3 of the valuation hierarchy. Certain unobservable inputs may, in isolation, have either a directionally consistent or opposite impact on the fair value of the finance instrument for a given change

Assets classified as held for sale are measured at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less estimated costs to sell, with any resulting adjustment recognized in selling, general and administrative expense in the condensed consolidated statements of operations. The assets’ highest and best use is as real estate land parcels for development or real estate properties for use or lease; however, the Company does not intend to develop or use these properties and plans to sell them to third parties as soon as practicable. Assets classified as held for sale are included in prepaid expenses and other assets on the condensed consolidated balance sheets.
The Company may be required, from time to time, to measure other certain assets and liabilities at fair value on a nonrecurring basis. The Company’s assets that are measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis and are evaluated with periodic testing for impairment include property, plant and equipment, operating lease right-of-use assets and operating lease liabilities, goodwill and other intangible assets. Estimates of the fair value of these assets and liabilities may rely on valuation methodologies developed using key inputs such as management's projections of future cash flows and discount rates. Accordingly, these fair value measurements are in Level 3 of the fair value hierarchy.
Assets and Liabilities Not Measured at Fair Value
The fair value of the Company’s cash and cash equivalents, restricted cash, accounts receivable, prepaid expenses and other assets and accounts payable and accrued liabilities approximate their respective carrying values due to the short-term nature.
Finance receivables at amortized cost, net consist of short-term and medium-term secured and unsecured consumer loans, including open end lines of credit. Loans originate at prevailing market rates. For the short-term secured and unsecured consumer loans, given the short-term nature of these loans and due to these loans continually being repriced at current market rates, the amortized cost approximates fair value. For the medium-term secured and unsecured consumer loans, the Company estimated fair value by using a discounted cash flow methodology. The internally developed model uses inputs, such as estimated loss, payment activity, discount rate, average loan age, and certain originating, servicing, and collection cost assumptions that are unobservable but reflect the Company's best estimates of the assumption a market participant would use to calculate fair value. The fair values of loans receivable are measured using Level 3 inputs.

The carrying value of the Company’s debt obligations approximates fair value. The Company’s term loans and revolving credit facilities, with both variable and fixed interest rates, are not actively traded and therefore do not have quoted market prices. The estimated fair values of these obligations are classified within Level 3 of the fair value hierarchy because the estimates incorporate significant unobservable inputs, including assumptions regarding the Company's credit risk and the terms of comparable financing arrangements. The Company’s variable interest rate debt facilities are generally tied to the Secured Overnight Financing Rate ("SOFR"), a market benchmark, with a short reset period, and as such, their carrying values approximate fair value. The estimated fair value of the Company's fixed-rate debt facilities is estimated by considering contractual interest rates, current market conditions and the terms and risk characteristics of comparable debt instruments. The estimated fair value approximates carrying value.

Consumer Finance Revenues
Finance receivable revenues consist primarily of interest income, origination fees, and finance charges associated with short-term and medium-term consumer loans. Origination fees and direct loan origination costs incurred for the origination of secured and unsecured short-term and medium-term consumer loans are deferred and recognized over the contractual term of the related loan using the effective interest method. Interest income earned from short-term and medium-term consumer loans is recognized over the term of the loan using the effective interest method for finance receivables at amortized cost. Finance receivables for which the fair value option has been elected are measured using a discounted cash flow methodology. Interest and fee income related to these receivables is recognized within consumer finance revenues and is distinct from changes in fair value.
Credit service fees are earned through the Company's CSO and credit access programs. Revenue is recognized over the period during which the Company fulfills its performance obligations, which generally corresponds to the arranged credit service period. The primary performance obligation is providing credit support and related services over the life of the arrangement.
Check cashing fees are recognized and the performance obligation is satisfied at the time the check cashing service is provided.
Other consumer finance service revenues include fees generated from card products, bill payment services, money transfers, money order sales, and other transaction-based services. Revenue is generally recognized at the point in time the related service is provided and the Company's performance obligation is satisfied. The transaction price is reduced for variable consideration related to assuring the minimum cash requirement and program fees paid directly to the third-party lending program provider. The Company estimates the amount of variable consideration to which it expects to be entitled at contract inception using the expected value, subject to the constraint that a significant revenue reversal is not probable and is reassessed each reporting period. For arrangements in which the Company acts as an agent, revenue is recognized on a net basis equal to the amount retained by the Company.

Lease Revenues
Lease revenues and fees consist primarily of amounts earned from lease-purchase agreements. The Company's lease arrangements are accounted for as operating leases under ASC 842, Leases ("ASC 842"). In accounting for its customer lease agreements as operating leases, the Company has considered that (1) the leases do not transfer ownership of the underlying asset to the lessee by the end of the lease term; (2) the leases do not grant the lessee an option to purchase the underlying asset that the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise; (3) the lease term is not for the major part of the remaining economic life of the underlying asset; (4) the present value of the sum of the lease payments does not equal or exceed substantially all of the fair value of the underlying asset; and (5) the underlying asset is not of a specialized nature that it is expected to have no alternative use to the Company at the end of the lease term.
The Company provides lease merchandise, consisting of furniture, appliances, electronics, computers, and other home goods to its customers for lease under certain terms agreed to by the customer. The Company offers leases with flexible ownership plans that can be generally renewed weekly, bi-weekly, semi-monthly, or monthly up to 24 months and generally does not require deposits upon inception of customer agreements. The customer has the right to acquire ownership either through an early purchase option, promotional purchase option or through payment of all required lease payments through the end of the ownership plan. Customers may generally terminate lease agreements at the end of each renewal period without penalty.
Aaron's also offers customers the option to obtain a membership in the Aaron’s Club program. Benefits of the Aaron’s Club program include lease protection, health & wellness discounts, and dining, shopping and consumer savings. The Company also offers Aaron’s Protection Plus with additional lease protection benefits. These benefits are renewable period to period and are cancellable at any time by either party without penalty.
Lease revenues related to the leasing of merchandise, Aaron's Club membership fees, Aaron's Protection Plus fees, and similar offerings by the Katapult operations are recognized as revenue in the month they are earned. Payments received prior to the month earned are recorded as deferred revenue in the accompanying condensed consolidated balance sheets. Lease payments due but not received prior to month end are recorded as accounts receivable in the accompanying condensed consolidated balance sheets. Lease revenues are recorded net of a provision for returns and uncollectible renewal payments.
Revenues from leases that originated from third-party merchants are generally recorded net of sales taxes as sales tax is collected from each customer's lease payment and a sales tax payable is recorded for remittance to the respective state. For KPay transactions, all sales tax is paid by the Company upon purchase of the goods and is typically recorded in the cost basis of the capitalized lease merchandise.
Substantially all lease revenues and fees were within the scope of ASC 842 for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026. Included in lease revenues and fees above, the Company had $15.1 million for both the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, within the scope of ASC 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers ("ASC 606").
The Company also has existing agreements with its current Aaron's franchisees to govern the operations of franchised stores. Our standard agreement is for a term of ten years, with one ten-year renewal option. Franchisees are obligated to remit to us royalty payments of 6% of the weekly cash revenue payments received, which is recognized as the underlying franchisee sales occur and the related fees become due. The Company also charges fees for advertising efforts that benefit the franchisees, which are recognized at the time the related services are provided. Substantially all franchise royalties and fees are within the scope of ASC 606. Of the franchise royalties and fees, $2.3 million for both the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, are related to franchise royalty income that is recognized as the fees become due.
Other revenues primarily consist of sales of leased assets and related lease agreements to third parties, commissions earned through third-party relationships, and other miscellaneous revenue streams. Revenue is recognized when control of the underlying asset or service transfers to the customer in accordance with ASC 606.
Merchandise Sales
All merchandise sales are within the scope of ASC 606 during the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026.
Revenues from the retail sale of merchandise inventories are recognized at a point in time that the Company has satisfied its performance obligation and transferred control of the product to the respective customer. Revenues associated with retail sales transactions for which control has not transferred are deferred and are recorded within deferred revenue within the accompanying condensed consolidated balance sheets.

Retail sales at the BrandsMart business, both in store and online, are subject to a 30-day return policy. Accordingly, an allowance, based on historical returns experience, for sales returns is recorded as a component of retail sales in the period in which the related sales are recorded as well as an asset for the returned merchandise. The return asset and allowance for sales returns were $0.5 million and $0.1 million, respectively, as of September 30, 2026. The return asset and allowance for sales returns was recorded within prepaid expenses and other assets and accounts payable and accrued liabilities within the accompanying condensed consolidated balance sheets, respectively. Additional protection plans can be purchased by BrandsMart customers that provide extended warranty coverage on their product purchases, with payment being due for this protection at the point of sale. A third-party underwriter assumes the risk associated with the coverage and is primarily responsible for fulfillment. The Company is an agent to the contract and records the fixed commissions. These fixed commissions on the extended warranty coverages are included within merchandise sales in the accompanying condensed consolidated statements of operations on a net basis and are recognized at the point of sale.
Revenues from the retail sale of lease merchandise to individual consumers are recognized at the point of sale and are recorded within merchandise sales in the accompanying condensed consolidated statements of operations. Generally, the transfer of control occurs near or at the point of sale for retail sales. Retail sales of lease merchandise to individual Aaron's customers are not subject to a returns policy.
Revenues for the non-retail sale of merchandise to Aaron's franchisees are recognized when control transfers to the franchisee, which is upon delivery of the merchandise to the franchisee store, and are recorded within merchandise sales in the accompanying condensed consolidated statements of operations. All non-retail sales revenue is within the scope of ASC 606.

CCF Term Loan
On March 26, 2021, the Company entered into a $20.0 million secured term loan (the "CCF Term Loan"), which was subsequently increased to $110.8 million through a series of amendments. The CCF Term Loan shares collateral and covenant structures with the First Lien Facility (as defined below). The CCF Term Loan was amended during the third quarter of 2026 to extend the maturity date to January 1, 2029. The facility is secured by the collateral supporting the First Lien Facility, requires interest-only payments with a balloon payment at maturity, and includes mandatory prepayment requirements and financial covenants.

Sparrow Term Loan
On July 8, 2022, Sparrow Purchaser, LLC, a wholly-owned subsidiary of CCFI, entered into a $120.0 million term loan (the "Sparrow Term Loan") as part of the financing for the purchase price of CCFI's acquisition of Speedy Cash, Rapid Cash and Avio Credit Businesses from CURO Intermediate Holdings Corp. (the "CURO Acquisition"). On October 2, 2023, the Sparrow Term Loan was amended to update and add additional terms and conditions, including certain debt covenants and reporting requirements. In August 2026, the Sparrow Term Loan was amended to increase the maximum commitment by $25 million to $75 million, increase the blended interest rate to 16.6%, extend maturity to December 31, 2027, and revise required principal payments to $1.7 million quarterly and $0.7 million monthly. The facility is subject to revised amortization requirements pursuant to the August 2026 amendment.

Trident ATL Loan
On October 2, 2023, Project Trident Purchaser, LLC (“Project Trident”), a wholly-owned subsidiary of CCFI, entered into a $148.3 million acquisition term loan (the “Trident ATL Loan”) as part of the financing for the purchase price of the acquisition (the “TMX Acquisition”) of TMX Finance, LLC (“TMX Finance”). In August 2026, the Trident ATL Loan was amended to update certain reporting requirements in connection with the Mergers.

Aaron’s Term Loan
As part of the acquisition of Aaron’s by IQV Holdco, LLC (the “IQV Acquisition”), Aaron’s entered into a $125.0 million term loan agreement (the “Aaron’s Term Loan”) at closing. The facility is secured by Aaron’s assets and interests not pledged on a first-lien basis, and the obligations may be accelerated upon specified defaults. On July 30, 2025, Aaron’s executed the first amendment to the Aaron’s Term Loan to increase the delayed-draw term loan ("DDTL") maximum commitment by $3.3 million, from $35.0 million to $38.3 million. On October 23, 2025, Aaron’s executed a second amendment to incorporate definitions related to the Merger Agreement.

First Lien Facility
On March 26, 2021, a wholly-owned subsidiary of CCFI entered into a $200.0 million asset-based secured revolving credit facility (the "First Lien Facility"), with a non-bank lender. The facility is collateralized by cash and eligible receivables and is subject to borrowing base and concentration limits. Interest-only payments are made periodically with a balloon payment at maturity. The First Lien Facility had a weighted average interest rate of 16.0% at September 30, 2026. The First Lien Facility was most recently amended during the third quarter of 2026 to extend the draw period to November 30, 2026, extend the maturity date to November 30, 2027 and modify certain terms. The $180.0 million maximum commitment remained unchanged. The First Lien Facility contains customary covenants and conditions, certain mandatory prepayment provisions, customary default provisions, as well as financial covenants, including minimum liquidity, adjusted earnings before interest expense, income taxes, depreciation and amortization ("EBITDA"), net income requirements, and a tangible asset coverage ratio.

Sparrow Single-pay Facility
On July 8, 2022, a subsidiary of CCFI entered into a single-pay facility (the "Sparrow Single-pay Facility") as part of the financing for the purchase price of the CURO Acquisition. In July 2026, the Sparrow Single-pay Facility was amended to increase the interest rate to 15.5%, extend the maturity to March 31, 2028 and modify certain reporting requirements.

Other Debt Obligations
In March 2026, CCFI assigned its former subsidiary Creditcorp to a liquidation trust and issued a $10.0 million unsecured promissory note to fund the settlement of Creditcorp matters. Resolution of those matters was deferred under an agreement with the Small Business Administration pending the outcome of related litigation in DACO Investments, LLC v. SBA, No. 6:22-cv-01444 (W.D. La. May 27, 2022), which remains on appeal in the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. In the interim, the parties in DACO Investments, LLC reached an agreement in principle with the SBA in late 2025 to resolve the matter, but Creditcorp and the SBA were unable to agree on final terms for settlement. Creditcorp continues to explore options for resolution. Accrued interest of $0.5 million at September 30, 2026 and $0.4 million at December 31, 2025 is included in accounts payable and accrued liabilities on the Company’s condensed consolidated balance sheets.
Financial Covenants and Compliance
The Company’s debt agreements generally contain affirmative and negative covenants, borrowing-base requirements, financial maintenance covenants, restrictions on additional indebtedness and distributions, and customary events of default. Certain facilities require compliance with minimum liquidity, interest coverage, tangible asset coverage, adjusted EBITDA, net income, leverage, and portfolio-value requirements. The Company was in compliance with the applicable financial covenants as of September 30, 2026.
Note 8: INCOME TAXES
The Company computes its interim income tax provision in accordance with ASC 740, Income Taxes. Income tax expense for interim periods is based on the estimated annual effective tax rate, adjusted for discrete tax items recognized in the period in which they occur.
The Company recorded income tax benefit of $12.1 million and $47.6 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, respectively, compared to income tax benefit of $1.2 million and income tax expense of $5.4 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2025, respectively. The income tax benefit recorded during 2026 includes the impact of a discrete tax benefit from the release of a valuation allowance during the first quarter.
As a result of the Mergers, the Company's tax profile has changed significantly, including the mix of earnings across jurisdictions, deferred tax assets and liabilities, valuation allowance considerations, and the impact of acquisition-related transaction and integration costs. Accordingly, period-over-period comparisons of the Company's effective income tax rate may not be indicative of future results. The historical financial statements presented for periods prior to the acquisition reflect the results of CCFI as the accounting acquirer, while the post-transaction period includes the post-acquisition operations, tax attributes, and legal entity structure of the combined company.
Note 9: (LOSS) EARNINGS PER SHARE
The Company calculates basic and diluted net (loss) earnings per share attributable to common stockholders in accordance with ASC 260, Earnings Per Share. Basic (loss) earnings per share is computed by dividing net (loss) earnings by the weighted average number of shares of common stock outstanding during the period. The computation of earnings per share assuming dilution includes the potential dilutive effect of stock options and restricted stock units ("RSUs") (collectively, "share-based awards") as determined under the treasury stock method. Contingently issuable shares are included in basic and diluted net

Further, shares issued/attributable to Aaron's and Katapult Holdings' (pre-merger) equityholders, as the accounting acquirees, are included in weighted average shares outstanding prospectively beginning on August 11, 2026.
The Company's basic and diluted earnings per share calculations for all periods prior to the Mergers assumes that the weighted average number of common shares outstanding was 56.4 million, which is the number of Katapult Holdings common shares issued in exchange for CCFI equity interests (excluding CCFI MIP Equity) in connection with the Mergers on August 11, 2026.

Note 10: COMMITMENTS AND CONTINGENCIES
Legal Proceedings:
From time to time, the Company is party to various legal and regulatory proceedings arising in the ordinary course of business, certain of which have been described below. The Company establishes an accrued liability for legal and regulatory proceedings when it determines that a loss is both probable and the amount of the loss can be reasonably estimated. The Company continually monitors its litigation and regulatory exposure and reviews the adequacy of its legal and regulatory reserves on a quarterly basis. The amount of any loss ultimately incurred in relation to matters for which an accrual has been established may be higher or lower than the amounts accrued for such matters due to the inherent uncertainty in litigation, regulatory and similar adversarial proceedings, and substantial losses from these proceedings or the costs of defending them could have a material adverse impact upon the Company’s business, financial position, and results of operations.
At September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, the Company accrued $28.2 million and $22.0 million, respectively, for pending legal and regulatory matters for which it believes losses are probable and is management’s best estimate of its exposure to loss. The Company records these liabilities in accounts payable and accrued liabilities in the condensed consolidated balance sheets.
Those matters for which a loss is reasonably possible but not probable and those matters for which a reasonable estimate is not possible are not included within these estimated ranges and, therefore, the estimated ranges do not represent the Company’s maximum loss exposure.

Jacob Atkinson v. Aaron’s, LLC
In Jacob Atkinson v. Aaron’s, LLC dba Aaron’s Sales & Lease Ownership, LLC, No. 23-2-19649, filed in 2023, currently pending in Washington state court, plaintiff, on behalf of himself and a putative class, alleges that Aaron’s, LLC (“Aaron’s LLC”) violated Washington’s Equal Pay and Opportunity Act, RCW 49.58.110 because certain Aaron’s LLC's job postings did not include a wage scale or salary range. Plaintiff seeks injunctive and declaratory relief and damages for himself and the putative class. A motion to dismiss the operative complaint is pending, but the case is currently stayed awaiting a ruling on a case involving different parties but similar legal issues.
Greensboro Law Center
Greensboro Law Center has filed a series of 16 mass actions in state court in North Carolina against various TitleMax branded entities (collectively “TitleMax Entities”) on behalf of claimants alleging that North Carolina law should apply to loans obtained by the claimants from TitleMax branded stores located outside of North Carolina. Fifteen of the mass actions have been removed to federal court, and fourteen have had their claims compelled to arbitration. Those arbitrations are in varying stages of litigation, including pending vacatur or confirmation in federal court. Two mass actions have yet to be compelled to arbitration. Various other ancillary litigation regarding these disputes is pending in North Carolina and South Carolina courts. The Company intends to continue to defend itself vigorously in these matters, and the outcome of the proceedings is uncertain.
In re Pennsylvania Department of Banking and Securities (“DOBS”)
In 2024, the Pennsylvania Department of Banking and Securities (“DOBS”) filed an administrative proceeding (the Order to Show Cause, or “OSC”) against TitleMax of Delaware, Inc., TitleMax of Ohio, Inc., TitleMax of Virginia, Inc., TitleMax of South Carolina, Inc., TitleMax Funding, Inc., TMX Finance LLC, TMX Finance Corporate Services, Inc., CCFI Companies, LLC, and all successors or predecessors in interest, affiliates, subsidiaries, or parent companies (collectively, the “Respondent Entities”) alleging the Respondent Entities: (1) need a license from the state of Pennsylvania and (2) offer products that violate various Pennsylvania laws. In the OSC, DOBS sought an order requiring the Respondent Entities to show that they did not violate certain Pennsylvania interest rate laws. In 2025, the Chief Hearing Examiner presiding over the OSC issued a Proposed Adjudication and Order in favor of the Respondent Entities, and adverse to DOBS, as to all counts. In the third quarter of 2026, the Pennsylvania Banking and Securities Commission (the “Commission”) largely reversed the determinations made by the Chief Hearing Examiner and ruled that the Respondent Entities must pay penalties and restitution. The Respondent Entities filed an appeal of the Commission’s findings with the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania on October 26, 2026. The Company intends to continue to defend itself vigorously in this matter. The outcome of the proceeding is uncertain, and the Company cannot predict the timing or ultimate resolution of the Commission’s review or of any related appeals. An estimate of the possible loss cannot be made with reasonable accuracy.
DCA Litigation
In October 2024, Katapult Group, Inc. reached a settlement with DCS Advisory, LLC (“DCA”) to resolve any and all disputes that exist between the two parties for total consideration of $3.0 million with half paid at settlement and the remainder paid over the next two years. The case was formally discontinued, with prejudice in October 2024. All obligations under the settlement have been fully satisfied as of September 30, 2026.
FlexShopper Litigation
In 2024, FlexShopper, Inc. (“FlexShopper”) filed a complaint against Katapult Holdings, Inc. in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, Marshall Division. The complaint alleged patent infringement and sought an injunction as well as damages for alleged lost profits and willfulness. In March 2026, FlexShopper was sold to ReadySett, LLC, a subsidiary of Snap Finance. In June 2026, the Company entered into a Patent License Agreement with ReadySett, LLC, resolving previously pending patent litigation. Under the agreement, the Company agreed to pay a lump-sum amount in exchange for a perpetual license to certain FlexShopper patents and the dismissal of all litigation-related claims. The lump sum amount was paid during the third quarter of 2026.
The assessment as to whether a loss is probable or reasonably possible, and as to whether such loss or a range of such losses is estimable, often involves significant judgment about future events, and the outcome of litigation is inherently uncertain. Other than as described above, there is no material pending or threatened litigation against the Company that remains outstanding as of September 30, 2026.
Non-Cancelable Commitments
At September 30, 2026, the Company had non-cancelable commitments primarily related to certain advertising and marketing programs, software licenses, and hardware and software maintenance of $115.8 million. Payments under these commitments are scheduled to be $26.4 million in 2026, $37.4 million in 2027, $20.2 million in 2028, and $31.8 million thereafter.

Unfunded Loan Commitments

The Company maintains a separate reserve for credit losses on off-balance sheet credit exposures, including unfunded loan commitments, which is included in accounts payable and accrued liabilities on the consolidated balance sheets. The reserve for credit losses on off-balance sheet credit exposures is adjusted as a provision for credit losses in the consolidated statements of operations. The estimate includes consideration of the likelihood that funding will occur and an estimate of expected credit losses on commitments expected to be funded over its estimated life, utilizing the same models and approaches for the Company’s other loan portfolio segments described in Note 1, as these unfunded commitments share similar risk characteristics as its loan portfolio segments. As of September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, the liability for credit losses on off-balance sheet credit exposure included in accounts payable and accrued liabilities was $1.0 million and $2.0 million, respectively.
Note 11: RESTRUCTURING
During the third quarter of 2026, the Company initiated the Katapult Holdings Cost Optimization Restructuring Program designed to optimize its real estate footprint, consolidate disparate information technology systems and processes including those in human resources, advertising and finance and accounting. Management believes that this restructuring program will help the Company optimize its cost profile and generate incremental value for stockholders through cost rationalization and optimization. This program also includes potential labor optimization in overlapping functions within its operating segments, the centralization and optimization of corporate functions, as well as other duplicative third party spend costs reductions. The Company expects the program to end on December 31, 2027. Management expects future restructuring expenses (reversals) due to potential early buyouts of leases with landlords, as well as continuing variable occupancy costs related to closed stores, to extend beyond that date.
Restructuring costs incurred during the third quarter of 2026 also include costs incurred following the Mergers associated with the historical Aaron’s Company Operational Efficiency and Optimization Restructuring Program, implemented in 2022, and primarily consisted of continuing variable occupancy costs incurred related to previously closed Aaron's stores.
Total net restructuring expenses under the Company's restructuring programs, which were recorded within the selling, general and administrative expense line in the condensed consolidated statements of operations, amounted to $11.1 million for both the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026. Such expenses were comprised mainly of operating lease right-of-use asset impairment charges, fixed asset impairment charges, severance, professional advisory fees, and continuing variable occupancy costs incurred related to closed stores.
As management continues to execute on its long-term strategic plan, additional benefits and charges are expected to result from our restructuring programs. The extent of future restructuring charges is not currently estimable and depends on various factors including the timing and scope of future cost optimization initiatives.

Treatment of Historical CCFI Awards
The issuance of Katapult Holdings common stock attributable to CCFI’s historical equity interests represents the recapitalization of the accounting acquirer and was not treated as consideration transferred. The Company evaluated the Merger Date treatment of the historical CCFI awards under ASC 718, Compensation—Stock Compensation, including whether any portions represented pre-combination compensation, transaction consideration or post-combination compensation expense. In connection with the Mergers, outstanding CCFI phantom restricted units were terminated in accordance with their applicable plan and award terms, and the holders became entitled to receive an aggregate of approximately 2.4 million shares of Katapult Holdings common stock, with delivery of such shares deferred for twelve months following the closing of the Mergers. The Company recognized non-cash equity-based compensation expense of $15.5 million in connection with the settlement of these awards, which was included in selling, general and administrative expense in the condensed consolidated statements of operations.
Treatment of Historical Aaron's Awards
As Aaron’s is an accounting acquiree, the fair value of awards attributable to service rendered before the Mergers was included in consideration transferred, to the extent required under ASC 805 and ASC 718.
Treatment of Historical Katapult Holdings Awards
At the closing of the Mergers, outstanding Katapult Holdings stock options, restricted stock unit awards and performance stock unit awards generally remained outstanding in accordance with their applicable award terms, except for awards that were settled, modified or otherwise treated pursuant to the Merger Agreement. Certain unvested restricted stock units held by former Katapult Holdings directors were settled in cash at closing. The cash settlement attributable to those director awards was included in consideration transferred. The portion of the fair value of other Katapult Holdings awards attributable to pre-combination services was included in consideration transferred, while the portion attributable to post-combination service will be recognized as stock-based compensation expense over the remaining requisite service period.
Purchase of Katapult Holdings Preferred Stock and Exercise of Katapult Holdings Private Warrants
On August 11, 2026, a subsidiary of Katapult Holdings entered into a term loan agreement for a senior secured term loan facility in an aggregate principal amount of $74.7 million to fund the purchase of Katapult Holdings' historical preferred stock. Additionally, in connection with the Mergers, Katapult Holdings' historical private warrants were exercised on a cashless basis in full for approximately 0.6 million shares of Katapult Holdings common stock. Following the exercise, no private warrants remained outstanding.

2026 Equity Incentive Plan
The Katapult Holdings, Inc. 2026 Equity Incentive Plan (the "2026 Plan") was approved by the Company's stockholders on August 6, 2026 and became effective in connection with the Mergers. The 2026 Plan authorizes the issuance of up to 9.0 million shares of the Company's common stock in connection with equity-based compensation awards to eligible participants. Following approval of the 2026 Plan, no additional awards may be granted under Katapult Holdings' prior 2021 Equity Incentive Plan; however, awards previously granted under the 2021 Equity Incentive Plan remain outstanding in accordance with their existing terms. As of September 30, 2026, 6.3 million shares remained available for future issuance under the 2026 Plan.

Stock-Based Compensation Expense
Stock-based compensation expense was $17.9 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 and is included in selling, general and administrative expense in the condensed consolidated statements of operations. As of September 30, 2026, there was $20.3 million of unrecognized stock-based compensation expense, which is expected to be recognized over a weighted-average period of 1.86 years.
Note 13: SEGMENTS
The Company reports information about its operating segments in accordance with the authoritative guidance related to segments. The Company manages and reports its operating results through two reportable segments: Consumer Finance and Lease-to-Own & Retail. These reportable segments align with how the Company's Chief Executive Officer, who is the Chief Operating Decision Maker (CODM), allocates resources, assesses performance and reviews financial information. The CODM
45

NOTES TO UNAUDITED CONDENSED CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

uses segment gross profit and segment operating profit to make decisions regarding the allocation of resources (including financial resources and capital spending) to each segment primarily in the annual budget and forecasting process and reviews budget to actual variances for segment operating profit on a monthly, quarterly and annual basis to assess the performance of each segment. The CODM does not evaluate performance or allocate resources based on segment asset data, and therefore total segment assets are not presented.
Consumer Finance Segment
The Company's Consumer Finance segment includes the operations of Community Choice Financial, Inc. Through its network of retail locations and digital platform, the Consumer Finance segment provides customers a variety of financial products and services, including secured and unsecured, short-term and medium-term consumer loans, check cashing, prepaid debit cards, and other services.
Lease-to-Own & Retail Segment
The Company's Lease-to-Own & Retail segment includes the operations of legacy Katapult and Aaron's.
The Lease-to-Own & Retail segment provides consumers with LTO and retail purchase options through the Company's Aaron's stores, along with its franchisees, in the United States and Canada and the aarons.com e-commerce platforms. In addition, the Lease-to-Own & Retail segment includes the operations of BrandsMart U.S.A., which is one of the leading appliance and consumer electronics retailers in the southeastern United States and one of the largest appliance retailers in the country with stores in Florida and Georgia and a growing e-commerce presence on brandsmartusa.com. Katapult, one of the Company’s operating brands, is a technology-driven LTO platform that integrates with omnichannel retailers and e-commerce platforms to provide nonprime consumers in the U.S. with access to everyday durable goods. Consumers who may be unable to access traditional financing can choose LTO at checkout with integrated retailers, or shop a growing network of merchants through Katapult’s mobile app marketplace and check out using its innovative Katapult Pay (“KPay”) feature.
