Note 14: RELATED PARTY TRANSACTIONS
As discussed in Note 2, CCFI has been designated as the accounting acquirer in the Mergers. The following details the related party transactions for the Company, the majority of which existed in 2025 when CCFI was a private company. Those prior relationships are disclosed under the heading "Prior CCFI Related Party Transactions" to distinguish them from ongoing transactions discussed under the heading "Ongoing Related Party Transactions".
Prior CCFI Related Party Transactions
A subsidiary of the Company is party to an unsecured swingline agreement (the “Swingline Loan”) with an entity controlled by IQ Business Finance, which provides the Company's subsidiary with short-term liquidity with a maximum borrowing capacity of $20.0 million. A family trust of a current board member and executive officer held an interest in the lender until September 2025, when that interest was sold. Following the sale, the Company's subsidiary did not have any interest accrued for the Swingline Loans as a related party. Interest expense on the Swingline Loan while a related party was $0.7 million and $1.1 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2025, respectively. These expenses are included in interest expense, net on the Company’s condensed consolidated statements of operations. Additional details for the Swingline Loan can be found in Note 7.
A subsidiary of the Company is party to an employee leasing agreement with Meridian Servicing, LLC (formerly IQV Servicing LLC) (“Meridian”), which provides employee leasing of personnel and other services related to loan servicing, collections, and technology. A family trust of a current board member and executive officer held a minority ownership interest in Meridian until September 2025, when the family trust sold the entirety of its interest. As a result, Meridian is no longer a related party, and there were no amounts due to Meridian as a related party as of September 30, 2026 or December 31, 2025. Expenses incurred for these services while Meridian was a related party were $10.4 million and $31.4 million for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2025, respectively. These expenses are included in selling, general and administrative expense on the Company’s condensed consolidated statements of operations.

Note 15: TRANSACTIONS WITH VARIABLE INTEREST ENTITIES
The Company evaluates its relationships with other entities under ASC 810 to determine whether it holds a variable interest in a variable interest entity (“VIE”) and, if so, whether it is the primary beneficiary. The Company has concluded that it is not the primary beneficiary of the VIEs described below and does not consolidate them.
Certain subsidiaries of the Company refer customers to unaffiliated third-party lenders under the CSO program and have agreed to reimburse the lenders for loans, and related fees, not collected from those customers. As of September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, the outstanding amount of loans guaranteed by the Company, which represents the Company’s maximum exposure, was $222.8 million and $239.2 million, respectively. The CSO interest and fee receivables were $41.2 million and $43.9 million at September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, respectively, and were included in finance receivables at amortized cost, net on the Company's condensed consolidated balance sheets. The related accrual for third-party lender losses of $43.9 million and $49.8 million, respectively, is included in accounts payable and accrued liabilities on the Company’s condensed consolidated balance sheets. The Company has determined that the lenders are VIEs but is not their primary beneficiary because it does not have the power to direct the activities that most significantly affect their economic performance.
Certain subsidiaries of the Company participate in a third-party lending program, supported by an unaffiliated third-party fund, that is offered to customers in the Company’s stores. In exchange, the Company assures a minimum cash requirement held by the fund. The liability for the minimum cash requirement was $3.8 million and $3.9 million as of September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, respectively, and is included in accounts payable and accrued liabilities on the Company’s condensed consolidated balance sheets. The Company has determined that only the fund is a VIE, and that only the minimum cash requirement expense and corresponding liability relate to it. The Company is not the primary beneficiary of the fund for the same reason described above. As of September 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025, the maximum exposure, representing the loans outstanding, was $36.5 million and $37.9 million, respectively.

ITEM 2. MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS

The following discussion and analysis of the financial condition and results of operations (this “MD&A”) of Katapult Holdings, Inc. (for purposes of this MD&A, “Katapult Holdings, Inc.”, the “Company,” “we,” “us” and “our”) should be read in conjunction with Katapult Holdings, Inc. unaudited Condensed Consolidated Financial Statements as of and for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, including the notes to those statements, appearing elsewhere herein. This MD&A contains forward-looking statements that involve risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by such forward-looking statements. Factors that could cause actual results to differ materially include, but are not limited to, those discussed under “Risk Factors.”
Business Overview
Katapult Holdings, Inc. (“Katapult” or the “Company”) is a scaled, technology and data-driven platform serving nonprime consumers seeking greater financial flexibility. On December 11, 2025, the Company entered into an Agreement and Plan of Merger (the “Merger Agreement”) with CCF Holdings, LLC ("CCFI"), Aaron’s Intermediate Holdco, Inc. ("Aaron’s") and two wholly owned indirect subsidiaries of the Company, Katapult Merger Sub 1, Inc. and Katapult Merger Sub 2, LLC, pursuant to which those subsidiaries merged with and into Aaron's and CCFI, respectively (the "Mergers"). Upon completion of the Mergers on August 11, 2026 (the "Merger Date"), CCFI and Aaron’s became wholly owned indirect subsidiaries of the Company. Under the terms of the Merger Agreement, equityholders of CCFI and Aaron’s received shares of the Company’s common stock, resulting in a change of control of the Company upon closing. The Mergers were accounted for as reverse mergers using the acquisition method of accounting, pursuant to ASC Topic 805, Business Combinations (“ASC 805”), with Katapult Holdings treated as the legal acquirer of CCFI and Aaron's and CCFI treated as the accounting acquirer of Katapult Holdings (pre-merger) and Aaron’s. See Note 2 to the accompanying condensed consolidated financial statements for additional information regarding the Mergers and related agreements.
Through its CCFI, Aaron's, and Katapult operating brands, we provide access to alternative consumer financial services and lease-to-own ("LTO") and retail solutions, bringing together proprietary data, technology and underwriting capabilities, retail and e-commerce capabilities, a nationwide physical footprint and customer-focused financial solutions to provide our consumers with the tools they need to navigate everyday life.
Consumer Finance Segment
CCFI is a provider of alternative financial services to unbanked and underbanked consumers that operates under various brands including TitleMax, Speedy Cash, CheckSmart and Community Choice Financial. CCFI owns and operates 1,588 retail locations in 25 states and is licensed to deliver similar financial services over the internet in 29 states as of September 30, 2026. Through its network of retail locations and over the internet, CCFI provides customers a variety of financial products and services, including secured and unsecured, short-term and medium-term consumer loans, check cashing, prepaid debit cards, and other services that address the specific needs of its individual customers.
Lease-to-Own and Retail Segment
Aaron's wholly owns The Aaron's Company, Inc. and is a leading, technology-enabled, omnichannel provider of LTO and retail purchase options of furniture, electronics, appliances, and other home goods across its brands: Aaron's and BrandsMart U.S.A. ("BrandsMart"). Aaron's provides consumers with LTO and retail purchase options through its approximately 1,160 Aaron's owned and franchised stores and showrooms in the United States and Canada and the aarons.com e-commerce platform. BrandsMart is a leading appliance and consumer electronics retailer in the southeast United States and one of the largest appliance retailers in the country with 11 stores in Florida and Georgia and a growing e-commerce presence on brandsmartusa.com and other internet marketplaces.

Katapult, one of the Company’s operating brands, is a technology-driven LTO platform that integrates with omnichannel retailers and e-commerce platforms to provide nonprime consumers in the U.S. with access to everyday durable goods. Consumers who may be unable to access traditional financing can choose LTO at checkout with integrated retailers, or shop a growing network of merchants through Katapult’s mobile app marketplace and check out using its innovative Katapult Pay (“KPay”) feature.

Reverse Merger and Basis of Presentation
The accompanying condensed consolidated financial statements as of and for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026, and the comparable prior‑year periods, reflect the financial position, results of operations, and cash flows of the Company and its wholly owned subsidiaries, with intercompany balances and transactions eliminated, and have been prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP.
As CCFI was deemed the accounting acquirer under reverse merger accounting, the historical financial statements of CCFI became the historical financial statements of the Company upon the consummation of the Mergers. As a result, the financial statements included in this report reflect (i) the historical operating results of CCFI and its consolidated subsidiaries prior to August 11, 2026 (the presentation of which has been reclassified to conform to the financial statement presentation of the Company subsequent to the Mergers); (ii) the consolidated results of the Company (including the operations of Katapult Holdings, CCFI and Aaron's) from the August 11, 2026 closing date forward; (iii) the assets and liabilities of CCFI at their historical cost; (iv) the assets acquired and liabilities assumed of Aaron's and Katapult Holdings (pre-merger) at fair value from the Merger Date; and (v) the Company’s equity structure for all periods presented.
In accordance with applicable guidance, the equity structure has been restated in all comparative periods to reflect the number of shares of the Company's common stock issued to CCFI unitholders in connection with the Mergers as if such shares had been held since the beginning of the earliest period presented. Further, shares issued to Katapult Holdings' and Aaron's stockholders in connection with the Mergers are treated as consideration transferred and are included in shares outstanding prospectively from the date of the Mergers.
The preparation of the Company's condensed consolidated financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP for interim financial information requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the amounts reported in these financial statements and accompanying notes. Actual results could differ from those estimates.
The accompanying unaudited condensed consolidated financial statements do not include all information required by U.S. GAAP for complete financial statements. In the opinion of management, all adjustments considered necessary for a fair statement have been included in the accompanying unaudited condensed consolidated financial statements. The results of operations for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026 are not necessarily indicative of operating results that may be achieved for another interim period or for the full year.
Within the MD&A, certain columns and rows may not add due to the use of rounded numbers for disclosure purposes. Percentages presented are calculated from the underlying whole-dollar amounts.

Key Components of (Loss) Earnings Before Income Taxes
For the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025 the key revenue, cost and expense components affecting (loss) earnings before income taxes were as follows:

Revenues. Revenues consist of consumer finance revenues, lease revenues and merchandise sales.
52

Consumer finance revenues primarily consist of interest income, origination fees and finance charges on consumer loans; credit service fees earned through credit services and credit access programs; check cashing fees; and fees from other consumer financial services, including card products, bill payments, money transfers and money orders.
Lease revenues primarily consist of revenues and fees from lease-purchase agreements at the Aaron’s and Katapult brands. Lease revenues also include franchise royalties and other revenues, including commissions, third-party property leasing and other miscellaneous revenue streams.
Merchandise sales primarily consist of retail merchandise sales from BrandsMart operations, including related warranty commissions, sales of new and pre-leased merchandise at Aaron’s stores, and non-retail merchandise sales to Aaron’s franchisees.

Costs of Revenues. Costs of revenues consist of consumer finance costs, lease revenue costs and merchandise sales costs.
Cost of consumer finance revenues primarily consists of fair value adjustments and net charge-offs related to finance receivables measured at fair value and provisions for credit losses related to finance receivables measured at amortized cost and certain guaranteed loans.
Cost of lease revenues primarily consists of depreciation of lease merchandise and other lease-related costs, including accelerated depreciation associated with early purchase transactions, as well as provisions for lease merchandise write-offs.
Cost of merchandise sales primarily consists of the cost of merchandise sold through BrandsMart and Aaron’s stores and to Aaron’s franchisees, including inventory and merchandise costs, freight and distribution costs, inventory markdowns, shrink and obsolescence, and other directly attributable merchandise costs.

Selling, General and Administrative Expenses. Selling, general and administrative expenses consists primarily of personnel costs, marketing costs, occupancy costs, depreciation and amortization, other operating expenses, restructuring expenses, and acquisition-related costs. Personnel costs include compensation, benefits and other employee-related costs. Operating expenses include collections related expenses, bank and credit card fee, professional services, technology, facilities, insurance and other administrative costs. Marketing includes advertising and customer acquisition costs. Depreciation and amortization primarily relates to property and equipment and finite-lived intangible assets. Restructuring expenses includes right-of-use asset and fixed asset impairments, severance and continuing occupancy costs related to closed stores incurred in conjunction with our restructuring programs. Acquisition-related costs primarily include professional and consulting fees and transaction-related compensation costs associated with the Mergers.

Other Expense (income). Other expense (income) primarily consists of non-operating expenses and income that are not included in the Company’s primary operating activities.

Interest Expense, net. Interest expense, net primarily consists of interest expense resulting from fixed and variable rate borrowings as well as the amortization of debt issuance costs and other financing arrangements, net of interest income earned on cash and other interest-bearing assets.

Revenues
Total consolidated revenues were $753.9 million and $443.3 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. This increase was driven by a $305.1 million increase in revenues in the Lease-to-Own & Retail segment due to the inclusion of the segments' results beginning with the August 11, 2026 completion of the Mergers and a $5.5 million increase in revenues in the Consumer Finance segment. See "Segment Performance" section below.
Gross Profit
Consolidated gross profit was $437.7 million and $280.0 million during the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. The increase in gross profit during the three months ended September 30, 2026 was primarily driven by a $157.0 million increase in the Lease-to-Own & Retail segment due to the inclusion of the segments results beginning with the August 11, 2026 completion of the Mergers. The Consumer Finance segment was relatively flat.

As a percentage of total consolidated revenues, consolidated gross profit decreased to 58.1% during the three months ended September 30, 2026 compared to 63.2% for the comparable period in the prior year primarily due to the inclusion of the Lease-to-Own & Retail segment results and the resulting impact on revenue mix, driven by lower gross profit margin for lease revenues and merchandise sales than consumer finance revenues.

We measure liquidity in terms of our ability to fund the cash requirements of our business, including working capital needs, the funding of finance receivables and merchandise purchases, operating expenses, capital expenditures, contractual obligations, debt service and other commitments. As of September 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of $261.0 million and approximately $130.4 million of available borrowing capacity under our credit facilities, subject to applicable borrowing base calculations, financial covenants and other conditions. We expect to fund our liquidity and capital requirements over the next 12 months primarily through existing cash and cash equivalents, cash flows from operations and, as necessary, borrowings under our credit facilities. We believe our existing sources of liquidity will be sufficient to meet our anticipated liquidity requirements for at least the next 12 months. Our future liquidity and capital requirements will depend on a number of factors, including our operating and financial performance, the availability of borrowing capacity under our credit facilities and economic, commercial, regulatory and financial conditions. If necessary, we may seek additional sources of liquidity, which could include additional indebtedness, asset-specific financing, asset sales or other capital transactions. Critical Accounting Estimates

Our critical accounting estimates are those estimates made in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (“GAAP”) that involve a significant level of estimation uncertainty and have had, or are reasonably likely to have, a material impact on our condensed consolidated financial statements. Actual results may differ materially from these estimates due to changes in facts, circumstances and assumptions.

Our significant accounting policies and acquisitions are described in Note 1 and Note 2 to the accompanying condensed consolidated financial statements. We believe that the following accounting policies affect the most significant estimates and management judgments used in preparing the consolidated financial statements.

Allowance for Credit Losses and Other Reserves for Third-Party Losses

Allowance for credit losses represents our estimate of expected losses over the life of finance receivables measured at amortized cost. Our other reserves for third-party losses associated with the CSO product offered through unaffiliated third-party lenders represent our estimate of expected losses related to defaulted loans subject to a guarantee. These estimates are inherently subjective and require significant judgment and rely on assumptions about future economic conditions and evaluation of credit risk.

We estimate allowance for credit losses and other third-party reserves using internal inputs such as historical loss experience, current conditions, delinquency, overall portfolio quality, and current economic conditions. Changes in these variables can materially affect our allowance for credit losses.

We estimate the allowance balance and other third-party reserves using relevant information relating to past events, current expectations related to economic conditions, and reasonable and supportable forecasts. The Company utilizes a loss rate approach in determining its lifetime expected credit losses primarily based on the Company’s historical loss experience. The Company’s current expected credit loss vintage model segments its loan portfolio into monthly pools of receivables by short-term, medium-term, secured and unsecured and estimates the allowance for credit losses by applying loss rates primarily derived from internal, historical cumulative loss experience, then adjusted by qualitative factors to address recent and forecasted business trends. Qualitative factors considered when determining any adjustments to the historical loss rates included, but were not limited to, contractual delinquency, the value of underlying collateral, economic and other qualitative considerations, and our judgment. We evaluate pooling decisions and adjust as needed from time to time as risk characteristics change. While we use the best information available to make our evaluation, future adjustments to the allowance for credit losses may be necessary if there are significant changes in economic conditions.

Finance Receivables at Fair Value

We have elected the fair value option for our medium-term secured and medium-term unsecured loan products, excluding line of credit and third-party lender products. We estimate the fair value of these finance receivables using a discounted cash flow methodology. Loss and payment activity and certain originating servicing, and collection cost assumptions are determined using respective historical data and include consideration of recent trends and anticipated future performance. Future cash flows are discounted using a rate of return that the Company believes is reflective of the market. The models are updated at each measurement date to capture any changes in internal factors such as nature, term, volume, payment trends, remaining time to maturity, and portfolio mix, as well as changes in underwriting or observed trends expected to impact future performance.

The following describes the primary inputs to the discounted cash flow analyses that require significant judgment:

•Net collections rate: The net collections rate includes all payments of principal, interest, fees, and recoveries developed using our historical experience on a portfolio vintage level and applied to the current portfolio to determine the expected future period cash flow.
•Cost assumptions: The cost assumptions include certain acquisition, servicing, and collections costs. These costs reflect our estimate of the amount we would incur to originate as well as service and collect the underlying assets over the assets’ remaining lives. These costs are derived from our historical experience.
•Discount rate: The discount rate utilized in the discounted cash flow model reflects our estimate of the rate of return that a market participant would require when investing in financial instruments with similar risk and return characteristics.



63

Income Taxes

Deferred income taxes are recorded to reflect the tax consequences in future years of differences between the tax basis of assets and liabilities and their financial reporting amounts, based on enacted tax laws and statutory tax rates applicable to the periods in which the differences are expected to affect taxable income. Valuation allowances are established when necessary to reduce deferred tax assets to the amounts expected to be realized. Income tax expense represents current tax obligations and the change in deferred tax assets and liabilities.

We recognize the tax benefit from an uncertain tax position only if it is more-likely-than-not that the tax position will be sustained on examination by taxing authorities, based on the technical merits of the position. The tax benefits recognized in the financial statements from such a position are measured based on the largest benefit that has greater than 50% likelihood of being realized upon ultimate settlement.

As of September 30, 2026, after evaluating all available positive and negative evidence, including sustained profitability and anticipated future earnings, we concluded that it is more likely than not that certain deferred tax assets will not be realized. We will continue to evaluate the realizability of our deferred tax assets on a quarterly basis.

Business Combinations

We account for business combinations using the acquisition method of accounting, which requires that once control is obtained, all the assets acquired and liabilities assumed are recorded at their respective fair values at the date of acquisition. Goodwill is measured as of the acquisition date as the excess of consideration transferred over the net acquisition-date fair value of the net identifiable assets acquired and liabilities assumed. During the measurement period, which is up to one year from the acquisition date, the Company may record adjustments to the assets acquired and liabilities assumed with the corresponding offset to goodwill due to the use of preliminary information in our initial estimates. Subsequent to the measurement period, any adjustments are recorded to earnings.

The determination of fair values of identifiable assets and liabilities requires estimates and the use of valuation techniques when fair value is not readily available and requires a significant amount of management judgment. For the valuation of intangible assets acquired in a business combination, we typically use an income approach. Specifically, for the Mergers, we used the relief-from-royalty method for developed technology and the Katapult Holdings trade names and trademarks and the multi-period excess earnings method for merchant relationships and the Aaron's trade names and trademarks. The significant assumptions used to estimate the fair value of intangibles included forecasted revenues and expenses, growth rates, royalty rates, attrition rates, and discount rates.

Although the Company believes its estimates of fair value are reasonable, actual financial results could differ from those estimates due to the inherent uncertainty involved in making such estimates. Changes in assumptions concerning future financial results or other underlying assumptions could have a significant impact on the determination of the fair value of the intangible assets acquired.

Recent Accounting Pronouncements

ITEM 3. QUANTITATIVE AND QUALITATIVE DISCLOSURES ABOUT MARKET RISK
Our future income, cash flows and fair values relevant to financial instruments are dependent upon prevailing market interest rates. Market risk refers to the risk of loss from adverse changes in market prices and interest rates. The primary market risk we are exposed to is interest rate risk. We do not use any significant market risk sensitive instruments to hedge commodity, foreign currency or other risks, and hold no market risk sensitive instruments for trading or speculative purposes.
Interest rate risk
Our exposure to market risk from adverse changes in interest rates is primarily associated with our loans carried at fair value and our debt instruments.
Beginning July 1, 2024, we elected the FVO for all newly originated medium-term secured and medium-term unsecured loans, excluding products tied to a line of credit and any third-party lender products under a CSO program. The changes in fair value are reported in the cost of consumer finance revenues on the Company’s condensed consolidated statements of operations. The fair value of the portfolio is measured based on a discounted cash flow methodology. Future cash flows are discounted using a rate of return that the Company believes is reflective of the market. A hypothetical increase of 100 basis points to the discount rates used in our valuations would decrease the balance of finance receivables at fair value by $1.2 million at September 30, 2026.
Market risk associated with our fixed-rate debt relates to the potential reduction in fair value from an increase in interest rates. Market risk associated with our variable-rate debt relates to the potential adverse effect on future earnings from an increase in interest rates. As of September 30, 2026, we had $1.9 billion of borrowings outstanding under our term loan and revolving credit facilities, further described in Note 7 to the accompanying condensed consolidated financial statements. Based on the underlying rates and outstanding balances at September 30, 2026, a hypothetical increase of 100 basis points in average annual interest rates would have increased the annual interest expense on our variable-rate debt by $10.6 million.
Concentration of credit risk
We deposit cash with financial institutions, and, at times, such balances may exceed federally insured limits. We believe the financial institutions that hold our cash and cash equivalents are financially sound and, accordingly, minimal credit risk exists with respect to cash and cash equivalents.
Inflation Risk
Although we believe that inflation has indirectly impacted our business by negatively impacting consumer spending and the sales of our key merchants, we do not believe that inflation has directly had, or currently directly has, a material effect on our results of operations or financial condition.
65

ITEM 4.CONTROLS AND PROCEDURES

Disclosure Controls and Procedures

Our management, with the participation of our Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer, evaluated the effectiveness of the design and operation of our disclosure controls and procedures (as defined in Rules 13a-15(e) and 15d-15(e) under the Exchange Act) as of September 30, 2026. Disclosure controls and procedures are designed to provide reasonable assurance that information required to be disclosed in the reports we file or submit under the Exchange Act is recorded, processed, summarized and reported within the time periods specified in the SEC's rules and forms. They are also designed to ensure that such information is accumulated and communicated to our management, including our Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer, as appropriate to allow timely decisions regarding required disclosure. Based upon their evaluation, our Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer concluded that our disclosure controls and procedures were effective as of September 30, 2026 at the reasonable assurance level.

Changes in Internal Control Over Financial Reporting

On August 11, 2026, we completed the Mergers, as a result of which CCFI and Aaron’s became wholly owned indirect subsidiaries of the Company. The Mergers were accounted for as a reverse merger, with CCFI treated as the accounting acquirer, and, accordingly, the historical financial statements of CCFI became the historical financial statements of the Company. In connection with the Mergers, we have implemented new processes and internal controls to assist us in the preparation and disclosure of financial information. These include controls over the accounting for the Mergers and the related preliminary purchase price allocation, and over the consolidation of, and financial reporting for, the CCFI, Aaron's and Katapult businesses. We are in the process of integrating the internal controls and processes of CCFI, Aaron's and Katapult businesses, and we expect to continue to evaluate and, where appropriate, modify our internal control over financial reporting as integration activities continue. We are evaluating the scope of management's assessment of internal control over financial reporting for the year ending December 31, 2026 in light of the Mergers.

Other than as discussed above, there were no changes in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting, as defined in Rule 13a-15(f) under the Exchange Act, during the quarter ended September 30, 2026 that have materially affected, or are reasonably likely to materially affect, the Company’s internal control over financial reporting.

PART II – OTHER INFORMATION
ITEM 1.LEGAL PROCEEDINGS
Jacob Atkinson v. Aaron’s, LLC
In Jacob Atkinson v. Aaron’s, LLC dba Aaron’s Sales & Lease Ownership, LLC, No. 23-2-19649, filed in 2023, currently pending in Washington state court, plaintiff, on behalf of himself and a putative class, alleges that Aaron’s, LLC (“Aaron’s LLC”) violated Washington’s Equal Pay and Opportunity Act, RCW 49.58.110 because certain Aaron’s LLC's job postings did not include a wage scale or salary range. Plaintiff seeks injunctive and declaratory relief and damages for himself and the putative class. A motion to dismiss the operative complaint is pending, but the case is currently stayed awaiting a ruling on a case involving different parties but similar legal issues.
Greensboro Law Center
Greensboro Law Center has filed a series of 16 mass actions in state court in North Carolina against various TitleMax branded entities (collectively “TitleMax Entities”) on behalf of claimants alleging that North Carolina law should apply to loans obtained by the claimants from TitleMax branded stores located outside of North Carolina. Fifteen of the mass actions have been removed to federal court, and fourteen have had their claims compelled to arbitration. Those arbitrations are in varying stages of litigation, including pending vacatur or confirmation in federal court. Two mass actions have yet to be compelled to arbitration. Various other ancillary litigation regarding these disputes is pending in North Carolina and South Carolina courts. The Company intends to continue to defend itself vigorously in these matters, and the outcome of the proceedings is uncertain.
In re Pennsylvania Department of Banking and Securities (“DOBS”)
In 2024, the Pennsylvania Department of Banking and Securities (“DOBS”) filed an administrative proceeding (the Order to Show Cause, or “OSC”) against TitleMax of Delaware, Inc., TitleMax of Ohio, Inc., TitleMax of Virginia, Inc., TitleMax of South Carolina, Inc., TitleMax Funding, Inc., TMX Finance LLC, TMX Finance Corporate Services, Inc., CCFI Companies, LLC, and all successors or predecessors in interest, affiliates, subsidiaries, or parent companies (collectively, the “Respondent Entities”) alleging the Respondent Entities: (1) need a license from the state of Pennsylvania and (2) offer products that violate various Pennsylvania laws. In the OSC, DOBS sought an order requiring the Respondent Entities to show that they did not violate certain Pennsylvania interest rate laws. In 2025, the Chief Hearing Examiner presiding over the OSC issued a Proposed Adjudication and Order in favor of the Respondent Entities, and adverse to DOBS, as to all counts. In the third quarter of 2026, the Pennsylvania Banking and Securities Commission (the “Commission”) largely reversed the determinations made by the Chief Hearing Examiner and ruled that the Respondent Entities must pay penalties and restitution. The Respondent Entities filed an appeal of the Commission’s findings with the Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania on October 26, 2026. The Company intends to continue to defend itself vigorously in this matter. The outcome of the proceeding is uncertain, and the Company cannot predict the timing or ultimate resolution of the Commission’s review or of any related appeals. An estimate of the possible loss cannot be made with reasonable accuracy.
DCA Litigation
In October 2024, Katapult Group, Inc. reached a settlement with DCS Advisory, LLC (“DCA”) to resolve any and all disputes that exist between the two parties for total consideration of $3.0 million with half paid at settlement and the remainder paid over the next two years. The case was formally discontinued, with prejudice in October 2024. All obligations under the settlement have been fully satisfied as of September 30, 2026.
FlexShopper Litigation
In 2024, FlexShopper, Inc. (“FlexShopper”) filed a complaint against Katapult Holdings, Inc. in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, Marshall Division. The complaint alleged patent infringement and sought an injunction as well as damages for alleged lost profits and willfulness. In March 2026, FlexShopper was sold to ReadySett, LLC, a subsidiary of Snap Finance. In June 2026, the Company entered into a Patent License Agreement with ReadySett, LLC, resolving previously pending patent litigation. Under the agreement, the Company agreed to pay a lump-sum amount in exchange for a perpetual license to certain FlexShopper patents and the dismissal of all litigation-related claims. The lump sum amount was paid during the third quarter of 2026.
The assessment as to whether a loss is probable or reasonably possible, and as to whether such loss or a range of such losses is estimable, often involves significant judgment about future events, and the outcome of litigation is inherently uncertain. Other than as described above, there is no material pending or threatened litigation against the Company that remains outstanding as of September 30, 2026.
