ITEM 1A.RISK FACTORS

The following risk factors supplement, and should be read together with, the risk factors described in Part I, Item 1A, “Risk Factors,” of the Company’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025 (the “2025 Form 10-K”), in Part II, Item 1A, “Risk Factors,” of the Company’s Quarterly Reports on Form 10-Q for the quarters ended March 31, 2026 and June 30, 2026 (the “2026 Form 10-Qs”), and in the Company’s other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”). Additional disclosure regarding risks may be found in the section titled “Risk Factors” of the proxy statement/prospectus included in the Company's Registration Statement on Form S-4 (File No. 333-296909), as amended (the “Form S-4”), which was declared effective by the SEC on July 7, 2026.

Except as set forth below, there have been no material changes to the risk factors disclosed in the 2025 Form 10-K or the 2026 Form 10-Qs. The risks described below and in the Company’s other filings are not the only risks the Company faces. Additional risks not currently known to the Company or that it currently deems immaterial may also materially and adversely affect its business, financial condition, results of operations and the trading price of its common stock.

Risks Related to the Mergers and the Integration of the Acquired Businesses

The Company may be unable to successfully integrate the businesses of Katapult, CCFI and Aaron’s, and may not realize the anticipated benefits of the Mergers, including anticipated synergies and cost savings, within the anticipated time frame or at all.

The success of the Mergers will depend, in large part, on the Company’s ability to combine the businesses of Katapult, CCFI and Aaron’s, which operated as independent companies until the completion of the Mergers, and to realize the anticipated benefits of the Mergers, including synergies, cost savings, innovation and operational efficiencies. The integration process is complex, costly, time-consuming, and requires significant management involvement. Potential difficulties include, among other things, integrating operations, corporate functions, technologies and customer service platforms; integrating marketing programs, data and analytics platforms and customer data; integrating information, accounting, finance, billing, payroll, reporting and regulatory compliance systems; implementing a unified business strategy and consistent operational, financial and managerial controls; eliminating duplicative operations and inconsistencies in standards, procedures and policies; and coordinating geographically dispersed organizations. Many of these factors are outside the Company’s control, and any one of them could result in delays, increased costs, decreased revenues and diversion of management’s time and attention. If the Company is unable to achieve the anticipated benefits within the anticipated time frame, or at all, its business, financial condition, results of operations and the market price of its common stock could be materially and adversely affected.

The integration of the acquired businesses may disrupt the Company’s ongoing operations and its relationships with customers, merchants, franchisees, vendors, lenders and other business partners.

The Company’s management must devote significant time and attention to integrating Katapult, CCFI and Aaron’s, which diverts attention from day-to-day operations and other opportunities and could result in performance disruptions at one or more of the Company’s businesses. Customers, merchants, franchisees, vendors, lenders, and other business partners may experience uncertainty about the combined company and, as a result, may delay or defer business decisions, seek to terminate, change or renegotiate their relationships with the Company, or decline to enter into new agreements with it. Regulators and licensing authorities may also subject the combined company to heightened scrutiny following the Mergers, which could result in additional examinations, delays in approvals or additional compliance requirements. In addition, as the Company centralizes certain operations, the potential impact of systems failures and other operational disruptions may become more significant. Any of these developments could adversely affect the Company’s revenues, earnings, cash flows and the market price of its common stock.

The Company’s success depends on its ability to retain, attract and motivate management personnel and other key employees, and post-closing uncertainty may make it more difficult to do so.

The Company’s success depends in part on the experience and industry knowledge of the management and other key employees of each of Katapult, CCFI and Aaron’s, including sales, marketing, data science, engineering, store and field personnel. Current and prospective employees may experience uncertainty about their roles within the combined company, and integration activities, changes in responsibilities, cultural differences and the elimination of duplicative functions may adversely affect morale and cause departures. Competition for senior executives and highly skilled employees is intense, and some competitors for talent may have greater resources. The Company may incur additional costs to retain and motivate key personnel, and no assurance can be given that it will be able to do so to the same extent that Katapult, CCFI and Aaron’s did previously. The loss of members of the Company’s leadership team or other key employees, or a failure to recruit qualified successors, could disrupt operations, impair the integration and the execution of the Company’s business strategy, and have a material adverse effect on its business, financial condition and results of operations.

68

The Company has incurred and expects to continue to incur substantial expenses related to the Mergers and the integration of the acquired businesses, which may exceed the savings from the synergies it expects to achieve.

The Company has incurred, and expects to continue to incur, substantial expenses in connection with the Mergers and integration, including advisory, legal, accounting, financing, severance, retention, systems and facilities consolidation costs. A large number of processes, policies, procedures, operations, technologies and systems must be integrated, including purchasing, accounting and finance, sales, payroll, pricing, compliance, risk management, marketing and benefits. Factors beyond the Company’s control could affect the amount or timing of these expenses, many of which are difficult to estimate accurately, and integration may result in additional unanticipated costs. These costs may exceed the savings the Company expects to achieve from eliminating duplicative costs and realizing other efficiencies, particularly in the near term.

The Company may not effectively manage its significantly expanded operations or successfully execute the business strategies of its combined businesses.

As a result of the Mergers, the Company’s business is significantly larger and more complex than the business of Katapult, CCFI or Aaron’s individually, and the Company’s management team has limited experience operating a combined business of this size and scope. Managing the expanded business will depend, in part, on management’s ability to implement operational, financial and strategic initiatives that address both the integration of three previously independent companies and the increased scale and complexity of the combined business. These initiatives require significant investment, may divert resources from other initiatives and may not generate the expected customer engagement, revenue or cost savings, and related restructuring charges may vary materially from the Company’s estimates. If the Company fails to manage its expanded operations or execute its strategies on a timely basis, its business, financial condition, results of operations and the market value of its common stock could be materially and adversely affected.

If the Company fails to establish and maintain effective internal control over financial reporting and disclosure controls and procedures across the combined company, its ability to report its financial results accurately and on a timely basis could be impaired.

The Company is required to maintain effective disclosure controls and procedures and internal control over financial reporting under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 and the rules of the SEC and Nasdaq. As private companies, CCFI and, since October 2024, Aaron’s were privately held companies not subject to the SEC’s internal control reporting requirements. A predecessor to Aaron’s reported a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2023, and Katapult Holdings (pre-merger) has also previously identified material weaknesses in its internal controls. The Company must integrate the accounting systems and controls of Katapult, CCFI and Aaron’s, expand its accounting and finance functions, and complete the evaluation, testing and any required remediation of the combined company’s controls, which will require substantial cost and management effort and may not be completed in a timely manner. If the Company identifies material weaknesses or otherwise fails to maintain effective controls, it may be unable to produce timely and accurate financial statements, investors may lose confidence in its reported financial information, the market price of its common stock could decline, and it could be subject to sanctions or investigations by Nasdaq, the SEC or other regulatory authorities.

Risks Related to the Company’s Indebtedness and Liquidity

The Company has substantial indebtedness following the Mergers, which may limit its operating flexibility, increase its borrowing costs and reduce its ability to withstand adverse developments.

The Company had approximately $1.95 billion of consolidated indebtedness outstanding as of September 30, 2026. The Company’s level of indebtedness could, among other things, require it to dedicate a significant portion of its operating cash flow to debt service; increase its vulnerability to downturns in its business, its industries or the economy; limit its ability to obtain additional financing, pay dividends or repurchase shares; and place it at a competitive disadvantage relative to less leveraged competitors. Higher interest rates also increase the cost of the Company’s variable rate indebtedness and future financings.

The Company’s debt agreements contain restrictive covenants, and a failure to comply with them, or to refinance its indebtedness when it matures, could result in the acceleration of its obligations and foreclosure on its assets.

The Company’s debt agreements contain affirmative, negative and financial maintenance covenants, which vary among its debt instruments and include, among others, minimum liquidity, interest coverage, leverage, net worth, tangible net worth, tangible asset coverage and maximum total debt requirements. The negative covenants limit, among other things, the Company’s ability to incur additional indebtedness, pay dividends, make investments, create liens, sell collateral, merge or dispose of substantially all of its assets and enter into certain affiliate transactions, and could limit its ability to pursue growth strategies. Compliance may be affected by events beyond the Company’s control. Prior to the Mergers, Katapult Holdings from time to time was unable to comply with certain financial covenants under certain of its debt instruments and relied on waivers from its lenders, and there can be no assurance that the Company’s lenders will grant waivers in the future. In addition, the Company’s ability to
69

refinance its indebtedness as it matures will depend on market conditions and its financial performance, and it may be unable to refinance on acceptable terms or at all. If the Company breaches a covenant and cannot obtain a waiver, its lenders could terminate their commitments, accelerate all outstanding obligations and foreclose on their liens against substantially all of its assets, and the Company could be unable to continue its operations or avoid bankruptcy. In addition, there can be no assurance that the Company will be able to refinance, extend or repay any of its credit facilities or term loans on acceptable terms or at all when they mature, including with respect to our Katapult SPV-1 LLC Revolving Line of Credit, First Lien Facility and Sparrow Term Loan, which are scheduled to mature in December 2026, November 2027, and December 2027, respectively. Any of these events would have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.

The Company may need to raise additional capital, which may not be available on acceptable terms or at all, and any such financing could dilute its stockholders or restrict its operations.

The Company relies on the banking, credit and capital markets to fund working capital, finance its lease and loan portfolios, refinance existing indebtedness and support its strategic initiatives. Credit market disruptions, tightening credit conditions, instability in the banking sector or negative rating agency actions could limit the Company’s ability to draw on its credit facilities, refinance its indebtedness or obtain new financing on favorable terms, if at all, and could increase its cost of capital. If adequate funds are not available, the Company may be required to defer capital expenditures and acquisitions, reduce discretionary spending or forgo growth opportunities. Any equity financing could result in significant dilution, and new securities may have rights senior to those of the Company’s common stock, while any new debt financing may involve covenants that further restrict its operations.

Risks Related to the Company’s Customers, Credit Performance and Business Operations
The Company’s customers are primarily nonprime and underbanked consumers, and adverse macroeconomic conditions could reduce demand for its products and services and impair its customers’ ability to make payments.

The Company generates substantially all of its revenue from lease payments, loan interest and fees and other transactions with consumers who generally lack sufficient cash or credit to obtain goods or financing through traditional channels, and it bears the risk of non-payment or late payment by these customers. Adverse macroeconomic conditions, including persistent inflation, a higher cost of living, rising interest rates, rising unemployment, declining consumer confidence, changes in state and federal regulatory enforcement activities, geopolitical conflicts, tariffs and uncertain trade policies, supply chain constraints, changes in immigration enforcement practices and labor shortages, may disproportionately affect these customers. Such conditions may reduce demand for the Company’s merchandise, leases, loans, check cashing and other financial services, lower lease renewal rates and transaction volumes, and increase delinquencies, lease merchandise write-offs and loan charge-offs. Any of these conditions could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s business, financial condition and results of operations.

If the Company’s proprietary underwriting, scoring and decisioning models do not accurately predict customer performance, or if its allowances for credit losses and fair value estimates prove inadequate, its results of operations could be adversely affected.

The Company’s businesses rely heavily on proprietary scoring models and lease and credit risk decisioning tools to determine whether to extend credit or enter into leases and to assess the risk of customers whose charge-off rates are much higher than those of traditional lenders’ customers. These models assume that the behavior of prior customers is indicative of future performance and rely on applicant and third-party data that may be inaccurate, incomplete or unavailable. Unexpected changes in consumer behavior may reduce the models’ effectiveness and require more frequent adjustments and greater management judgment. If the models fail to perform as intended, the Company may approve customers who are unable to satisfy their obligations, increasing delinquencies, charge-offs and merchandise write-offs, or may overprice its products and lose customers. In addition, the Company’s allowances for credit losses and its estimates of the fair value of certain assets are based on assumptions and judgments that are inherently uncertain, and actual losses or fair values may differ materially from those estimates, which could require additional provisions for credit losses or write-downs.

The Company operates in highly competitive industries, and its inability to compete successfully could materially and adversely affect its business.

The Company faces intense competition from lease-to-own stores and websites, virtual lease-to-own and rent-to-rent companies, buy now, pay later providers, traditional and e-commerce retailers offering layaway, point-of-sale financing or other lending options, online and storefront consumer lenders, money services businesses and sellers of used merchandise. Competitors may have significantly greater financial and operating resources, greater name recognition and more developed products, e-commerce platforms and logistics networks. Some competitors may offer products on an unprofitable basis, relax their decisioning standards or engage in pricing or compliance practices that the Company will not, and prime lenders may loosen their underwriting standards to reach consumers with limited access to traditional banking and credit products. Merchants may also develop competing in-house lease-to-own or financing products. These pressures could compel the Company to reduce prices, cause it to lose market share and reduce its revenue and profitability.
70


The Company’s growth depends on its ability to attract and retain customers in a cost-effective manner.

Across its businesses, the Company’s ability to attract and retain customers depends on its brand and reputation, customer experience, product mix and the effectiveness of its marketing channels, including search engine marketing, preapproved direct mailings based on consumer reporting agency lists, paid media and third-party marketing firms. Regulatory restrictions on these channels, or increases in their cost or decreases in their effectiveness, could limit customer acquisition. The Company’s e-commerce platforms are also a significant component of its strategy, and the Company may be unable to maintain or grow them profitably. Any of these developments could adversely affect the Company’s business, financial condition and results of operations.

The Company’s revenue and operating results may fluctuate significantly from period to period, including due to seasonality.

The Company’s revenue and operating results may vary from quarter to quarter due to general economic conditions, customer spending patterns, holiday and seasonal sales and the timing of tax refunds. Results in the Lease-to-Own & Retail segment reflect higher first-quarter activity in its Aaron’s and Katapult lease-to-own businesses and higher fourth-quarter retail activity at BrandsMart. Consumer Finance segment results are affected by customers cashing tax refund checks, while its consumer loan business typically declines in the first six months of the year as customers receive tax refunds. Adverse events during the first or fourth quarter could have a disproportionate effect on the Company’s results for the year. Periods of decline could reduce the Company’s profitability, make it more difficult to service its indebtedness and cause its results to fall below the expectations of analysts and investors.

The Company depends on third-party financial institutions, payment processors, card networks and other service providers, and the loss of, or disruptions in, these relationships could disrupt its operations.

The Company relies on banks, payment processors, card issuers and networks and other third parties to fund leases and loans, disburse proceeds, collect payments, process debit card and automated clearing house (“ACH”) transactions and provide depository and treasury management services. For example, Katapult is required under its Loan Agreement to use a designated loan processor to validate customer purchases for funding, and leases originated through KPay are disbursed to merchants via single-use virtual cards issued through Marqeta and its issuing bank partner, Sutton Bank. As previously disclosed, American Express has notified Katapult that it will no longer serve as a processor. Card networks and processors may increase fees or modify their requirements, and noncompliance could result in fines or the suspension or termination of the Company’s registrations. Certain financial institutions have discontinued, and others may discontinue, providing banking, ACH and treasury management services to CCFI as a result of regulatory pressure or for other reasons. CCFI also depends on an issuing bank for its prepaid debit cards, Western Union and the unaffiliated lenders that originate loans under its credit services organization program. If any of these parties ceases or curtails its services or experiences errors or interruptions, the Company may be required to use its own cash to cover uncovered transactions and may be unable to find replacements on commercially reasonable terms, which could require it to materially alter or discontinue some of its operations.

CCFI’s access to the ACH system and to banking services could be impaired by changes to network operating rules or by regulatory pressure on financial institutions.

CCFI uses debit card processing and the ACH system both to deposit loan proceeds into customers’ bank accounts and to collect amounts due. The National Automated Clearinghouse Association has revised its operating rules to, among other things, establish an overall return rate threshold of 15% of an originator’s debit entries, limit certain reinitiated entries and impose fees on certain unauthorized returns. Future amendments could increase CCFI’s costs or limit its access to the ACH system. In addition, regulatory initiatives have previously discouraged banks and payment processors from serving consumer lenders. Although an August 2025 executive order and recent fair access legislation in Florida and Tennessee seek to limit such practices, financial institutions may still decline to provide services to CCFI, and the regulatory approach to these matters could change. If CCFI’s access to these systems and services is impaired, it may be required to materially alter or discontinue some or all of its business.

Operating a large network of retail stores and franchised locations exposes the Company to operational, inventory, product safety, franchisee and cash-handling risks.

Aaron’s has a decentralized, high fixed-cost operating model, driven by the labor demands of its selling, lease renewal and collections functions, last-mile delivery and fulfillment centers, which may result in negative operating leverage when revenues decline. Aaron’s must manage inventory to anticipate changing consumer preferences, often well in advance of seasonal demand, and must re-lease or sell returned merchandise. Aaron’s has experienced, and may continue to experience, merchandise cost increases from tariffs, commodity prices, supply chain disruptions and shipping costs that it may be unable to pass on to customers, as well as the commoditization of electronics and other product categories and reduced vendor discounts as purchase volumes decline. The products the Company leases and sells are subject to regulation by the U.S. Consumer
71

Product Safety Commission and similar authorities, and recalls could result in lost sales, lease terminations and increased costs. Aaron’s franchisees are independent businesses that the Company does not control, and their operational or financial difficulties could reduce franchise revenues and damage the Company’s brand, while franchisee disputes and franchise laws limiting termination or enforcement rights could result in costly litigation. In addition, because CCFI maintains significant cash in its stores, it is subject to losses from robbery, employee error and theft. For both Aaron’s and CCFI, rising rent on its store locations could increase its occupancy costs.

The Company depends on a large hourly workforce and is subject to laws governing wages, hours and working conditions, and increases in labor costs could adversely affect its results.

A substantial portion of CCFI’s and Aaron’s workforces consists of retail hourly employees in positions that have historically experienced high turnover and significant competition for workers, including from retail fulfillment centers, delivery services and restaurants. The Company is subject to the Fair Labor Standards Act, the National Labor Relations Act, immigration laws and various federal and state laws governing minimum wage, break requirements, overtime, exempt status classification, health benefits and working conditions. Increases in minimum wages, changes in exempt status classification, increases in benefit and workers’ compensation costs, and the costs of compliance and related litigation could increase the Company’s labor costs and adversely affect its business, financial condition and results of operations.

The geographic concentration of the Company’s assets and stores, natural disasters and other business disruptions, and the adequacy of its insurance could adversely affect its financial performance.

CCFI’s total gross receivables and Aaron’s operated and franchised stores, though diverse, do include some concentration in specific geographic regions. Adverse economic conditions, regulatory changes or severe weather in these regions, including hurricanes and flooding along the Gulf Coast, could disproportionately affect the Company’s results, and natural disasters, pandemics, acts of terrorism and other disruptions could destroy facilities, interrupt operations and reduce consumer spending. The Company self-insures certain risks, including portions of workers’ compensation, general liability, employee health and certain property risks, and its insurance is subject to deductibles, retentions, exclusions and limits that may be inadequate. Insurance and surety bonds may not be available on acceptable terms, insurers may refuse to renew policies or fail to meet their obligations, and changes in actuarial assumptions could result in significantly higher expenses than expected.

Fraudulent activity and misconduct or errors by the Company’s employees, franchisees, vendors and service providers could result in losses and harm its reputation.

The Company bears the risk of loss from customer identity fraud and other fraudulent activity in its lease-to-own and lending transactions, and it generally has no recourse to merchants to collect amounts owed by fraudulent customers. The Company’s internet operations are particularly susceptible to fraud because of the lack of face-to-face interaction and document review, and criminals use increasingly sophisticated methods, including impersonating the Company in attempts to collect debts from its customers. The Company’s fraud prevention tools may be insufficient, and it may be difficult or impossible to recover funds lost to fraud. The Company is also exposed to the risk that its employees, franchisees, vendors and service providers engage in misconduct or make errors, including misappropriating funds or data, improperly executing transactions, failing to follow compliance policies for originations, renewals and collections, engaging in discrimination or harassment, or violating anti-bribery laws such as the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Significant increases in fraud or misconduct, or even unsubstantiated allegations of misconduct, could result in direct losses, liability, regulatory intervention, negative publicity and erosion of customer and merchant trust.

CCFI’s revenue from check cashing, money services and prepaid debit card products may decline as a result of technological developments, regulatory changes, changes in economic conditions such as economic downturns or rises in unemployment, and collection losses.

The increasing adoption of direct deposit, electronic payroll and government benefit payments, prepaid debit cards and online payment platforms has displaced, and may continue to displace, the paper checks that customers cash in CCFI’s stores, and changes in the tax preparation industry could reduce the number of tax refund checks CCFI cashes. When CCFI cashes a check, it assumes the risk that it will be unable to collect from the payer due to insufficient funds, stop payment orders or fraud. In addition, provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act limiting debit card interchange fees, and the responses of card networks, issuers and processors, could reduce the revenue CCFI receives from distributing prepaid debit cards. Because a significant portion of CCFI’s check cashing business involves payroll checks, a prolonged economic downturn or rising unemployment could also reduce demand for these services.

72

Risks Related to Technology, Cybersecurity and Intellectual Property

Cybersecurity incidents affecting the Company’s systems or those of third parties on which it relies could result in significant costs, liability and reputational harm, and these risks are heightened by the integration of its information technology environments.

The Company’s businesses collect, process, store and transmit large amounts of personal and financial information of customers and employees, including Social Security numbers and bank account information, through retail stores, a mobile app, websites, merchant integrations and an online lending platform, and they rely on third-party service providers to process and store such information. The Company and these third parties are subject to evolving threats, including ransomware, malware, social engineering, denial-of-service and supply-chain attacks, personnel misconduct and error, and attacks by organized criminal and nation-state actors, which may be enhanced by the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning (“AI/ML”). The integration of the Company’s information technology environments may expose it to vulnerabilities present in the acquired businesses' systems. A security incident could disrupt operations, result in unauthorized access to or loss of confidential information, and subject the Company to notification obligations, regulatory investigations, fines, litigation (including class actions), indemnification obligations, loss of customers and reputational harm, and its insurance and contractual limitations of liability may not be adequate to cover these losses.

Failures or disruptions of the Company’s technology platforms, software and third-party data sources, and its use of AI/ML, could interrupt its business and expose it to liability.

The Company depends on its information technology systems, including Katapult’s proprietary platform, CCFI’s point-of-sale and management information systems and internet lending platform, and Aaron’s in-store and e-commerce decisioning and transaction processing systems, as well as third-party cloud infrastructure, software and data providers. Software errors, outages, telecommunications or power failures, operator error or catastrophic events could impair the Company’s ability to decision applications, process transactions, post payments and collect amounts owed, and its business continuity and disaster recovery plans may be inadequate. Third-party data providers on which the Company’s decisioning tools depend may experience outages, provide inaccurate data, increase their prices or cease providing data, including due to regulatory restrictions. The Company also uses AI/ML in key aspects of its businesses, including fraud analysis, credit risk analysis and pricing. If its AI/ML models are incorrectly designed or trained on incomplete, inaccurate or biased data, or if the Company lacks sufficient rights to that data, its products may not perform as intended and it could incur legal liability, reputational harm or regulatory scrutiny, and rapidly evolving AI/ML regulation may require the Company to modify its models or increase its compliance costs.

Legal, Regulatory and Reputational Risks

The Company’s businesses are subject to extensive and evolving federal, state and local laws and regulations, and its failure to comply with them could result in significant liability, restrictions on its operations and increased costs.

The Company’s lease-to-own, consumer lending and money services businesses are subject to extensive regulation, supervision and licensing by federal, state and local authorities, including the Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (the “CFPB”). These laws govern, among other things, interest rates, fees and other financial terms; lease-to-own pricing, disclosures, renewal and collection practices; loan amounts, durations and renewals; truth-in-lending, fair lending and equal credit opportunity; debt collection; credit reporting; military lending under the Military Lending Act and the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act; electronic funds transfers; anti-money laundering; and the offer and sale of franchises. In most jurisdictions, CCFI must be licensed, meet net worth requirements, post surety bonds and undergo periodic examinations, and state attorneys general and financial services regulators regularly scrutinize the Company’s products and practices and appear to have increased their scrutiny of the lease-to-own industry. These laws are subject to varying and at times inconsistent interpretation, and regulators and courts have considerable enforcement discretion. Violations could result in fines, penalties, restitution, refunds of principal, interest and fees, loss of licenses and orders requiring the Company to modify or discontinue products or practices, and the Company’s expanded footprint across states, products and distribution channels increases the complexity and cost of compliance.

The CFPB has broad supervisory and enforcement authority over the Company’s businesses, and certain of the Company's subsidiaries are subject to consent orders by the CFPB and other regulators.

The Dodd-Frank Act grants the CFPB broad authority to examine providers of consumer financial products, adopt rules declaring acts or practices unfair, deceptive or abusive, and pursue enforcement actions seeking restitution, rescission and civil money penalties that can exceed $1 million per day for knowing violations, and it empowers state officials to enforce certain federal consumer financial laws. The payment withdrawal and disclosure provisions of the CFPB’s 2017 rule governing payday, vehicle title and certain high-cost installment loans became operative on March 30, 2025, and if the CFPB prioritizes enforcement of those provisions, the Company may be unable to implement required changes effectively. In addition, certain of the Company's subsidiaries have consented to the issuance of consent orders by the CFPB and the FTC relating to Company's
73

business practices, under which it has agreed to pay restitution and civil money penalties and/or is subject to conduct restrictions for varying periods. Any noncompliance with these consent orders could result in further penalties and restrictions.

Changes in laws, regulations, or adverse regulatory actions could limit the Company’s products, reduce its revenues or make the continuation of certain of its businesses impractical, unprofitable or impossible.

Federal, state and local legislators and regulators have adopted or considered, and may adopt, measures such as caps on annual percentage rates for consumer loans, including a proposed federal 36 percent cap; limits on fees, loan amounts and rollovers; mandatory cooling-off periods and extended payment plans; ability-to-repay requirements; statewide loan databases; restrictions on lead generation and other marketing activities; legislation or regulations that would treat lease-to-own transactions as credit sales or loans or otherwise limit lease-to-own pricing, fees or renewal or collection practices; and local zoning and permit requirements. Voters in several states have approved ballot initiatives capping the interest rate on payday and certain other consumer loans at 36 percent. Several states in which CCFI operates or previously operated have enacted laws, or allowed laws to expire, in ways that adversely modified or eliminated its ability to offer certain loan products. In Texas, CCFI operates as a licensed credit access business under statutory provisions that, if changed, could force CCFI to discontinue or materially modify that program. Regulators may also interpret existing requirements in new ways; for example, in June 2024 the Pennsylvania Department of Banking and Securities initiated an administrative action against several CCFI subsidiaries relating to loans to Pennsylvania residents who traveled to other states to obtain loans, which has resulted in prolonged litigation. Any of these developments could have a material adverse effect on the Company’s business, financial condition and results of operations.

The Company’s lease-to-own and small-dollar lending products are controversial, and negative publicity or public perception of its businesses could reduce demand and lead to more restrictive regulation.

Consumer advocacy groups, the media, legislators and certain government agencies have characterized lease-to-own transactions and unsecured short-term, unsecured medium-term and direct secured consumer loans as predatory or abusive, often focusing on the cost of rental or on annual percentage rates. If these characterizations become increasingly accepted, demand for the Company’s products could decline significantly, and the Company could become subject to more restrictive laws, ballot initiatives or referenda and more stringent enforcement. Negative publicity regarding the Company, its competitors, its franchisees or its industries, including with respect to customer service, collection practices, data privacy and security practices, litigation or regulatory activity, even if inaccurate or related to isolated incidents, could spread through social media, erode customer and merchant trust, make it more difficult to attract and retain employees, and adversely affect the Company's business, financial condition and results of operations.

The Company is subject to litigation and regulatory proceedings, and limitations on the enforceability of its arbitration agreements could increase its litigation costs and exposure.

The Company is, and may in the future become, subject to lawsuits, class actions, regulatory proceedings and other claims, including challenges to the legality of its lending, leasing, collection and other business practices and claims relating to the Mergers. Adverse outcomes could require the Company to refund fees, interest and principal, pay multiple damages, penalties or significant settlements, post bonds or modify or terminate operations in particular states or nationwide, and defending these matters, even if successful, could be costly and divert management's attention. Others in the Company’s industries have paid material amounts to settle class actions and regulatory proceedings alleging violations of consumer protection and other laws. The Company generally requires customers and certain employees to enter into arbitration agreements containing class action waivers. Certain courts have found such agreements unconscionable and unenforceable, Congress and state legislatures have considered legislation that would limit or prohibit pre-dispute arbitration in consumer contracts, and a change in the judicial interpretation of the Federal Arbitration Act could affect the enforceability of such agreements. If the Company’s arbitration agreements become unenforceable, its exposure to class action litigation and its litigation costs could increase significantly.

Risks Related to Ownership of the Company’s Common Stock

Legacy Katapult Holdings stockholders have a significantly reduced ownership interest, a limited number of holders own a substantial portion of the Company's common stock, and future sales of its common stock could depress its market price.

As a result of the Mergers, legacy Katapult Holdings stockholders exercise significantly less influence over the Company's policies than they did prior to the Mergers. Holders of significant ownership stakes may have interests that differ from those of other stockholders and could delay or prevent a change of control. Sales of substantial amounts of the Company’s common stock, including shares registered for resale under registration rights agreements or issued upon the exercise of outstanding warrants or under its equity incentive plans, or the perception that such sales may occur, could depress the market price of its common stock and impair its ability to raise capital.

In addition, following the Mergers, a significant portion of the Company’s common stock is held by a limited number of holders, including former CCFI and Aaron’s equityholders, and shares held by directors, executive officers and holders of more
74

than 10% of its common stock are not considered publicly held under NASDAQ rules. As a result, the Company’s common stock may be less liquid and more volatile than that of more widely held companies, and small trades could cause significant price movements. A limited public float could reduce the Company’s eligibility for inclusion in stock indices, limit institutional investor interest and analyst coverage, make it more difficult to satisfy NASDAQ continued listing requirements relating to publicly held shares or to raise equity capital on favorable terms, and impair stockholders’ ability to sell shares at desired times or prices.
